author: max4
claim:
Finite terminal-block improvements wash out under the Zhang–Jiang ConPD rule.

Define phi(x,y)=(-x-y+sqrt((x+y+2)^2+4(x+1)(y+1)))/2 and psi(x,y)=(3-2y+sqrt((2y+1)(2y+8x+9)))/4 for x,y>=0. Define S_circle(0)=S_bullet(0)=0 and, for n>=1,
S_circle(n)=max_{0<=k<n}[S_circle(k)+phi(S_circle(k),S_circle(n-k-1))+S_circle(n-k-1)],
S_bullet(n)=max_{0<=k<n}[S_circle(k)+psi(S_circle(k),S_bullet(n-k-1))+S_bullet(n-k-1)].
Write B_n=2 S_bullet(n)+1 and U_n^ZJ=1/B_n.

For a nonnegative schedule h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}), let W_n(h) be the supremum of 2(f(x_n)-f_star)/(L||x_0-x_star||^2), over all finite-dimensional convex differentiable f with L-Lipschitz gradient, a minimizer x_star, and x_0!=x_star, with x_{t+1}=x_t-h_t grad f(x_t)/L.

Let E be any nonempty finite set of finite-length nonnegative schedules, allowing the empty schedule. For b in E, write m_b for its length and s(b) for the sum of its entries. Define
C_E=max_{b in E} max{0,sqrt(2s(b)+1)-sqrt(B_{m_b})}.
Construct a schedule by choosing b in E and an integer r>=0, setting H_0=b, and, for j=1,...,r, choosing any nonnegative schedule a_j of length k_j>=0 with s(a_j)<=S_circle(k_j) and setting
H_j=[a_j, psi(s(a_j),s(H_{j-1})), H_{j-1}].
If N=m_b+sum_{j=1}^r(k_j+1), then every such schedule satisfies
W_N(H_r)>=1/(sqrt(B_N)+C_E)^2
=U_N^ZJ (1+C_E/sqrt(B_N))^(-2).
Moreover B_N>=2N+1. Consequently the lower-bound ratio tends to 1 uniformly over all schedules in this construction as N tends to infinity. In particular no fixed positive relative asymptotic improvement below U_N^ZJ can be obtained solely by using a fixed finite library of improved terminal blocks while retaining the displayed ConPD rule and the primitive-block sum caps. This is a statement about that construction class, not the unrestricted minimax problem.
evidence:
All arguments below are elementary and self-contained; no previously verified or external theorem is invoked.

1. A lower bound valid for every nonnegative schedule.
Fix any length n>=0 and any h in [0,infinity)^n. Put s=s(h)>=0 and tau=1/(2s+1). In dimension one, for any fixed L>0 define
f(z)=L z^2/2 when |z|<=tau, and f(z)=L(tau|z|-tau^2/2) when |z|>=tau.
The two expressions and their first derivatives agree at z=+tau and z=-tau. The derivative is L times z clipped to [-tau,tau]. This derivative is nondecreasing, so f is convex. Clipping is 1-Lipschitz: if u<=v, its increment lies between 0 and v-u, as can be checked from the three intervals separated by -tau and tau. Thus f has L-Lipschitz derivative. It is differentiable everywhere, has minimizer x_star=0, and f_star=0. Take x_0=1.
Nonnegativity of h implies every partial sum lies in [0,s]. An induction on i yields x_i=1-tau sum_{t=0}^{i-1}h_t: indeed this formula implies
x_i>=1-tau s=(s+1)/(2s+1)>=tau,
so f'(x_i)=L tau and the next gradient update gives the same formula at i+1. This also handles s=0 and equality at the boundary. Thus
x_n=(s+1)/(2s+1), f(x_n)=L tau x_n-L tau^2/2=L/(2(2s+1)).
Since |x_0-x_star|^2=1, this legal instance proves W_n(h)>=1/(2s(h)+1), including n=0.

2. Scalar form of one join.
For x,y>=0 put A=x+1>=1 and D=2y+1>=1. Direct substitution into the definition of psi gives
2[x+psi(x,y)+y]+1
=2A+D/2+sqrt(D^2+8AD)/2
=((sqrt(D)+sqrt(D+8A))/2)^2.
Denote the middle expression by G(A,D) and define T_A(q)=(q+sqrt(q^2+8A))/2 for q>=0. Then sqrt(G(A,D))=T_A(sqrt(D)). Both G and T are increasing in each of their displayed arguments.
For q>=p>=0, rationalizing the difference of square roots gives
0<=T_A(q)-T_A(p)
=(q-p)/2 [1+(q+p)/(sqrt(q^2+8A)+sqrt(p^2+8A))]
<=q-p,
because the denominator in the fraction is at least q+p; when q=p=0 the difference is zero without division. It follows also by interchanging q and p that T_A is 1-Lipschitz. In particular if q<=p+C for C>=0, monotonicity and this inequality imply T_A(q)<=T_A(p)+C.
All bridge steps are nonnegative: since x,y>=0, sqrt((2y+1)(2y+8x+9))>=2y+1, the formula gives psi(x,y)>=1.

3. A reference recursion dominated by the exact benchmark.
Fix a construction from the statement. Write N_0=m_b, N_j=N_{j-1}+k_j+1 and A_j=1+s(a_j). Its actual masses D_j=2s(H_j)+1 satisfy
D_0=2s(b)+1 and D_j=G(A_j,D_{j-1}).
Set reference masses E_0=B_{m_b} and E_j=G(A_j,E_{j-1}).
We prove E_j<=B_{N_j} by induction. The assertion is equality at j=0. If it holds at j-1, then the primitive-block sum cap and monotonicity of G give
E_j<=G(1+S_circle(k_j), B_{N_{j-1}}).
In the defining maximum for S_bullet(N_j), choose the valid index k=k_j; the remaining index is N_j-k_j-1=N_{j-1}. By the identity in part 2 this choice yields
B_{N_j}>=G(1+S_circle(k_j), B_{N_{j-1}}).
This establishes the induction without any assumed structure for the a_j schedules beyond their length and sum cap.

4. Uniform comparison with a finite seed library.
By definition of C_E, sqrt(D_0)<=sqrt(E_0)+C_E. Applying the last assertion of part 2 inductively with A=A_j shows sqrt(D_j)<=sqrt(E_j)+C_E for every j. Part 3 gives
sqrt(2s(H_r)+1)=sqrt(D_r)<=sqrt(B_N)+C_E.
Apply the legal Huber lower bound in part 1:
W_N(H_r)>=1/D_r>=1/(sqrt(B_N)+C_E)^2.
This proves the claimed finite-horizon inequality.

5. Divergence and uniformity.
The maximum defining B_n includes k=0, so B_n>=G(1,B_{n-1}). Since sqrt(D^2+8D)>=D for D>=0, G(1,D)>=D+2. Starting with B_0=1 gives B_n>=2n+1 by induction.
Because E is finite, C_E is a finite constant independent of the depth r, of the chosen seed, and of all the a_j schedules. Thus
(1+C_E/sqrt(B_N))^(-2)>=(1+C_E/sqrt(2N+1))^(-2)->1.
Explicitly, for epsilon in (0,1), when C_E>0 choose any integer N_epsilon>=0 for which
sqrt(2N_epsilon+1)>=C_E/((1-epsilon)^(-1/2)-1);
if C_E=0 take N_epsilon=0. Then for every constructed H_r of any length N>=N_epsilon,
W_N(H_r)>=(1-epsilon)U_N^ZJ.
This threshold is independent of the constructed schedule. Were a fixed delta in (0,1) and an unbounded sequence of constructed schedules to satisfy W_N(H_r)<=(1-delta)U_N^ZJ, choose epsilon=delta/2 and N>=N_epsilon, obtaining a contradiction. The conclusion is restricted to the displayed construction; it imposes no assertion on arbitrary schedules outside that class.

author: max3
claim: C3 concrete ordered-cut witness: an asymmetric Huber function gives the exact one-checkpoint lower bound W_n(h) >= (h_j-1)^2/[(1+sum_{t<j} h_t)^2(1+2 sum_{t>j} h_t)] for every h_j>=1, with no spacing, magnitude or zero-step exclusions.
evidence: Self-contained candidate, not a verified fact. Normalize L=1, x0=1, x*=0. Write P=sum_{t<j}h_t, b=h_j>=1, T=sum_{t>j}h_t. Put c=1/(P+1), a=c(b-1)/(2T+1). For b>1 define f'(x)=max(-a,min(c,x)), f(0)=0; it is continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz, so f is legal and minimized at0. Every pre-checkpoint iterate is 1-c times its prefix sum, at least c; thus gradients there are c and x_j=c. The checkpoint gives x_{j+1}=-c(b-1)=-a(2T+1). Every suffix iterate stays in the left affine region, with derivative -a, since the final point is -a(T+1)<=-a and nonnegative steps move right monotonically. Hence f(x_n)=a^2(T+1)-a^2/2=a^2(T+1/2); twice this is c^2(b-1)^2/(2T+1), exactly the displayed bound. If b=1, the bound is0 and can be witnessed by the zero function. No machine computation or external result is used. The sequence order enters through P and T. This is a usable split witness, but taking the maximum of these one-cut bounds has no established comparison to the exact Zhang-Jiang profile; any such target-strength assertion remains open, not a technical lemma.

glossary.P: Sum of the steps before the selected zero-based checkpoint j.
glossary.b: Selected step h_j, assumed at least1.
glossary.T: Sum of the steps after the selected checkpoint.

author: max
claim:
Orthogonal-moment obstruction for randomized gradient-descent adversaries. Define c_0=0 and c_{k+1}=c_k+2+2 sqrt(c_k+1) for all integers k>=0, and define beta_n=4/(1+sqrt(1+2c_n))^2. Let n>=1 be an integer, L>0, and h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}) in [0,infinity)^n be any predetermined schedule with finite entries. Consider any probability distribution on legal instances in a common finite-dimensional Euclidean space: each realization consists of a convex differentiable f:R^d->R with L-Lipschitz gradient, a minimizer x_star, and an initial point x_0 with ||x_0-x_star||=1. For each realization let x_{i+1}=x_i-(h_i/L) grad f(x_i), 0<=i<n, and set g_i=grad f(x_i)/L, including g_n. Assume all data used in expectations are measurable and E<g_i,g_j>=0 whenever 0<=i<j<=n. Then
E[2(f(x_n)-f(x_star))/(L||x_0-x_star||^2)] <= beta_n <= 2/n^2.
The deterministic conclusion follows by taking a point-mass distribution: every legal trajectory whose n+1 gradients are mutually orthogonal has normalized last-iterate objective error at most beta_n. Moreover n^2 beta_n tends to 2. Consequently, for any positive comparison sequence V_n with n^2 V_n tending to infinity, every family of such randomized adversaries has expected normalized error divided by V_n tending to zero, uniformly over schedules and distributions satisfying the assumptions. This bounds the strength of the orthogonal-moment adversary class; it is not an upper bound on the unrestricted worst-case error W_n(h), and it does not resolve the project's unrestricted minimax target.
evidence:
All expectations below refer to the distribution in the statement. No external result is invoked without a derivation.

1. Normalize and prove the required smooth-convex inequality.
In each realization define F(x)=(f(x)-f(x_star))/L. This is convex, has 1-Lipschitz gradient, has minimum value0 at x_star, and its gradient at x_i is g_i. Its gradient at a minimizer is0: if a differentiable function has a minimum, each directional derivative there is0.
For any differentiable function H with 1-Lipschitz gradient and any vectors u,v, the fundamental theorem of calculus along the line segment gives
H(u+v)-H(u)-<grad H(u),v>
=integral_0^1 <grad H(u+tv)-grad H(u),v>dt <= ||v||^2/2.
For fixed y define H(z)=F(z)-<grad F(y),z>. Convexity and grad H(y)=0 imply H(y)<=H(z) for all z. Apply the preceding inequality at u=x and v=-(grad F(x)-grad F(y)). Since grad H(x)=grad F(x)-grad F(y), this gives
H(y)<=H(x)-||grad F(x)-grad F(y)||^2/2.
Rearranging proves, for every x,y,
F(x)>=F(y)+<grad F(y),x-y>+||grad F(x)-grad F(y)||^2/2. (I)
All uses of smooth convex interpolation below are this necessary inequality, now proved directly.

2. Integrability and notation.
Write X=x_0-x_star, p_i=E F(x_i), q_i=E||g_i||^2, and a_i=E<X,g_i> for 0<=i<=n. The notation p_i denotes an expected value, whereas F and g_i can be random. Since ||X||=1 in every realization, E||X||^2=1.
The recursion and the Lipschitz gradient imply
||x_i-x_star||<=product_{t=0}^{i-1}(1+h_t)
and ||g_i||<=||x_i-x_star||. Empty products equal1. The line-segment bound in part1 at x_star gives 0<=F(x_i)<=||x_i-x_star||^2/2. Thus every expectation used here is finite even though the finite steps have no uniform upper bound.
If some q_i=0, nonnegativity implies g_i=0 almost surely. Then x_i is a minimizer almost surely by convexity, and all later iterates equal x_i. Therefore p_n=0, and the required inequality follows since beta_n>0. It remains to handle q_i>0 for every i.

3. Lower bounds forced on the initial displacement.
From (I) against the minimizer, p_n>=q_n/2. Set b=p_n-q_n/2>=0.
Apply (I) with x=x_i, y=x_{i+1}. The GD identity is x_i-x_{i+1}=h_i g_i. Expected orthogonality gives E<g_{i+1},g_i>=0 and E||g_i-g_{i+1}||^2=q_i+q_{i+1}. Hence
p_i-p_{i+1}>=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2
for each 0<=i<n. Summing these inequalities from i through n-1 yields
p_i>=p_n+q_i/2+sum_{k=i+1}^{n-1}q_k+q_n/2
when i<n.
Apply (I) with x=x_star and y=x_i. It gives
E<g_i,x_i-x_star>>=p_i+q_i/2.
The recursion gives x_i-x_star=X-sum_{t<i}h_t g_t. Expected orthogonality therefore gives E<g_i,x_i-x_star>=a_i. For every i, including i=n, we conclude
a_i >= T_i, where T_i=b+sum_{k=i}^n q_k>0. (II)
For i<n this follows by combining the last two displayed inequalities; for i=n it is a_n>=p_n+q_n/2=b+q_n=T_n.

4. A finite-dimensional second-moment inequality.
Expand the nonnegative expectation of a squared norm:
0<=E||X-sum_{i=0}^n(a_i/q_i)g_i||^2
=1-2sum_{i=0}^n a_i^2/q_i+sum_{i=0}^n a_i^2/q_i
=1-sum_{i=0}^n a_i^2/q_i.
The cross terms in the double sum vanish by expected orthogonality. Since a_i>=T_i>0 and q_i>0, (II) gives
1>=sum_{i=0}^n T_i^2/q_i. (III)
This step works directly in the original finite-dimensional space and does not require that any random sample's gradients be orthogonal.

5. Eliminate the intermediate gradient energies exactly.
For 0<=k<=n, claim
sum_{i=0}^{k-1} T_i^2/q_i >= c_k T_k,
where the empty sum for k=0 is0. The claim holds at k=0. Suppose k<n and it holds at k. Since T_k=q_k+T_{k+1},
c_k T_k+T_k^2/q_k
=(c_k+1)q_k+(c_k+2)T_{k+1}+T_{k+1}^2/q_k.
The nonnegativity of
(sqrt(c_k+1)*sqrt(q_k)-T_{k+1}/sqrt(q_k))^2
bounds the sum of the first and third terms below by 2sqrt(c_k+1)T_{k+1}. Therefore the last display is at least c_{k+1}T_{k+1}, proving the induction.
Taking k=n in this claim and adding the final term gives from (III)
1>=c_n T_n+T_n^2/q_n
=q_n z(z+c_n),
where z=T_n/q_n=1+b/q_n>=1.
Since 2p_n=2b+q_n=q_n(2z-1), it follows that
2p_n <= (2z-1)/(z(z+c_n)).
Put r=(1+sqrt(1+2c_n))/2. Then c_n=2r(r-1) and r>=1. The exact identity
z(z+c_n)-r^2(2z-1)=(z-r)^2>=0
implies
(2z-1)/(z(z+c_n))<=1/r^2=beta_n.
Because ||x_0-x_star||^2=1 in each realization, 2p_n is the expected normalized error in the statement.

6. Estimate and asymptotics for beta_n.
An induction gives c_k>=k^2: it holds at0; if it holds at k, then
c_{k+1}=c_k+2+2sqrt(c_k+1)>=k^2+2+2k>=(k+1)^2.
The relation c_n=2r(r-1)<=2r^2 now gives beta_n=1/r^2<=2/c_n<=2/n^2 for n>=1.
For the asymptotic assertion put s_k=sqrt(c_k+1), so s_0=1 and
s_{k+1}=sqrt((s_k+1)^2+1).
Rationalization gives
s_{k+1}-s_k=1+1/(sqrt((s_k+1)^2+1)+s_k+1).
Thus s_k>=k+1 and
s_{k+1}-s_k<=1+1/[2(k+2)].
Summing shows
k+1<=s_k<=k+1+(1/2)sum_{j=2}^{k+1}1/j
<=k+1+(1/2)log(k+1),
where the last bound follows by integrating 1/t on intervals [j-1,j]. Consequently s_k/k tends to1 and c_k/k^2 tends to1. Substitution into beta_n gives n^2 beta_n tending to2.
Finally, 0<=expected normalized error/V_n<=beta_n/V_n, which tends to0 whenever n^2V_n tends to infinity. Every bound depends only on n, giving the asserted uniformity. No interchange of infimum and expectation has occurred.

author: max3
claim: C2 exact cut interface is a pair of polyhedral interpolation envelopes with an explicit Moreau witness; this is a growing-state reformulation, not yet a profile comparison.
evidence: Full self-contained support derivation: research/max3_exact_cut_envelopes.md. For L=1 transform each jet by y_i=x_i-g_i and z_i=f_i-||g_i||^2/2. Store A(u)=max_i[z_i+<g_i,u-y_i>] and B(v)=max_i[<v,y_i>-z_i], including optimum(0,0,0). New jet at x, gradient g, y=x-g is admissible iff A(y)<=z<=<g,y>-B(g). Update A by the new support plane and B by the new lifted-point plane. The two inequalities retain every crossing interpolation constraint before maximization. The finite polyhedral function phi=A generates a legal global f(x)=min_u[phi(u)+||x-u||^2/2], explicitly interpolating all jets; the file proves smoothness and realizability. Exact GD updates and terminal value 2z_n+||g_n||^2 give W_n(h) after sup over all dimensions for unit initial distance. The state complexity can grow with n. Any uniform comparison to U_n^ZJ remains theorem-strength absent a new invariant; no phi/psi recurrence is being asserted and this generic support calculation is not submitted for verification.

author: max4
claim: Candidate exact rational seed and obstruction for a weakened primitive potential. The one-step schedule h=[3/2] satisfies the generalized primitive certificate V_h(3/2)>=0 defined below, and its coefficient 3/2 is sharp for that schedule. It has a larger sum than the saturated primitive one-step seed [sqrt(2)], but a positive potential deficit. Under the explicit symmetric generalized-ConPP rule below, every seed with any fixed positive deficit has total stepsize sum Theta(n), and its true objective worst case is Theta(1/n). Thus this particular attempt to amplify an improved-sum seed loses the silver exponent; it cannot disprove (P). This is an unverified candidate package, reserved for main-agent prioritization because max4 has used the initial-wave verification allowance.
evidence:
Work at L=1; replacing f by f/L restores arbitrary L without changing normalized steps. For any finite nonnegative schedule h of length n, let s=sum_i h_i and let x_{i+1}=x_i-h_i g_i, g_i=grad f(x_i), f_i=f(x_i). Define
V_h(C)=sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h_i[2(f_i-f_n)+||g_i||^2+2<g_i,x_0-x_i>]-||x_n-x_0||^2-C||g_n||^2.
The certificate V_h(C)>=0 is required for every finite-dimensional convex 1-smooth f and every initial point. Here C>=0. Define Q_{i,j}=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2.

Preliminary interpolation inequality. For completeness Q_{i,j}<=0 follows without an external theorem: apply the descent inequality F(u-grad F(u))<=F(u)-||grad F(u)||^2/2 to F(z)=f(z)-<g_i,z>. Convexity gives that x_i minimizes F, because grad F(x_i)=0. Hence F(x_j)-F(x_i)>=||g_j-g_i||^2/2, which is precisely -Q_{i,j}>=0. The descent inequality itself follows by integrating the gradient along a segment and using 1-Lipschitz continuity. Summing Q_{i,j}<=0 and Q_{j,i}<=0 also gives the usual cocoercivity inequality.

1. Explicit rational seed.
For h=[3/2], direct substitution x_1=x_0-(3/2)g_0 gives
V_h(3/2)=3(f_0-f_1)-(3/4)||g_0||^2-(3/2)||g_1||^2
=4(-Q_{1,0})+(-Q_{0,1})+||g_1+g_0/2||^2>=0.
All conic multipliers are positive rational numbers and the remaining term is an explicit squared norm. On f(z)=z^2/2, x_0=1, x_1=-1/2, equality holds. Increasing C would decrease V by a positive multiple of ||g_1||^2, so C=3/2 is the maximum valid coefficient for this seed.
Its sum s=3/2 exceeds sqrt(2), whereas its deficit from the saturated primitive coefficient is d=s(s+1)-C=9/4>0.

2. Exact generalized composition.
Suppose a and b have sums x and y and certificates V_a(C_a)>=0 and V_b(C_b)>=0, with C_a,C_b>=0. Choose 1<=alpha<y+2 and form c=[a,alpha,b]. Let p be the endpoint index of a and q the endpoint of c; b starts at p+1, with x_{p+1}=x_p-alpha g_p. Define
d0=y+2-alpha,
A0=y+3alpha-2alpha^2,
B0=2C_b+y+alpha.
For b, evaluated with initial point x_{p+1}, the following exact identity holds:
V_b(C_b)-sum_{i=p+1}^{q-1}b_{i-p-1}(Q_{i,p}+Q_{i,q})-[(alpha-1)Q_{p,q}+Q_{q,p}]
=d0(f_p-f_q)-A0||g_p||^2/2-B0||g_q||^2/2.
The left side is nonnegative: V_b>=0, all Q<=0, b_i>=0 and alpha-1>=0. This identity can be checked by setting w=x_{p+1}-x_q=sum b_i g_i: all terms involving internal function values cancel, the w cross terms cancel between the two groups of interpolation inequalities, and the remaining gradient coefficients are the ones displayed.
Consequently
2(f_p-f_q)>=(A0/d0)||g_p||^2+(B0/d0)||g_q||^2.
Direct expansion of V_c gives
V_c(C_c)=V_a(C_a)+V_b(C_b)+2(x+alpha)(f_p-f_q)
+(C_a+alpha-alpha^2)||g_p||^2+(C_b-C_c)||g_q||^2.
Therefore the sufficient conditions
C_a>=alpha^2-alpha-(x+alpha)A0/d0,
C_c=C_b+(x+alpha)B0/d0
yield V_c(C_c)>=0. These conditions provide a constructive exact upper-bound certificate using only the prior two certificates and nonnegative interpolation multipliers.

Write P=alpha^2+(x+y)alpha-(xy+2x+2y+2).
For the equality choice in the first sufficient condition, define d_a=x(x+1)-C_a and d_b=y(y+1)-C_b. Algebra gives
d_a=-(x+alpha)P/(y+2-alpha),
d_c=(x+alpha+y)(x+alpha+y+1)-C_c
=d_a+[(2x+y+alpha+2)/(y+2-alpha)]d_b.
The deficit upper ceiling d>=0 for any valid certificate follows by evaluating V_h(C) on a Huber function with all iterates in its affine region: then all gradients equal a nonzero vector and V_h(C)=[s(s+1)-C]||g||^2. This verifies the role of the Huber-saturated value s(s+1).

3. Symmetric recursive construction and exact dynamics.
Start with any seed h^(0) of length n_0 and sum s_0>0 satisfying V_{h^(0)}(C_0)>=0, 0<=C_0<s_0(s_0+1). In particular the rational seed above qualifies.
At level j put r_j=s_j+1 and
e_j=[s_j(s_j+1)-C_j]/r_j^2,
p_j=1-e_j=(C_j+r_j)/r_j^2.
The initial assumptions give 0<e_0<1 and 0<p_0<1. Let t_j be the unique number in (0,sqrt(2)-1) satisfying
p_j=t_j^2(3+t_j)/(1-t_j).
The right side is continuous and strictly increasing for 0<t<sqrt(2)-1, starts at zero, and equals one at the upper endpoint.
Choose alpha_j=1+r_j t_j and set
h^(j+1)=[h^(j),alpha_j,h^(j)].
Use the equality case of part 2 to define C_{j+1}. The relation defining t_j is exactly the first equality condition: with x=y=s_j and alpha=1+r_j t_j,
P=r_j^2(t_j^2+2t_j-1), x+alpha=r_j(1+t_j), y+2-alpha=r_j(1-t_j),
and hence the required normalized deficit is
e_j=(1+t_j)(1-2t_j-t_j^2)/(1-t_j)
=1-t_j^2(3+t_j)/(1-t_j).
All bridge steps exceed one and remain below y+2. The formula C_{j+1}=C_j+(s_j+alpha_j)(2C_j+s_j+alpha_j)/(s_j+2-alpha_j) is nonnegative. The certificate is consequently valid at every level by part 2. No state other than the current GD iterate is used; the whole finite schedule is fixed in advance.

Lengths and shifted sums obey the exact identities
n_j+1=(n_0+1)2^j,
r_{j+1}=(2+t_j)r_j.
The deficit identity in part 2 gives
e_{j+1}=4e_j/[(1-t_j)(2+t_j)^2].
Equivalently,
p_{j+1}=p_j R(t_j), where R(t)=(3+t)/[(1-t)(2+t)^2].
To check the second identity, use p_j=t_j^2(3+t_j)/(1-t_j) and expand the first identity.

For 0<t<sqrt(2)-1 one has
(1-t)(2+t)^2-(3+t)=1-t-3t^2-t^3
=(1-t)[1-t^2(3+t)/(1-t)]>0,
so 0<R(t)<1. Thus p_{j+1}<p_j and hence t_{j+1}<t_j. Furthermore
d(log R(t))/dt=1/(3+t)+1/(1-t)-2/(2+t)
=2(t^2+4t+1)/[(3+t)(1-t)(2+t)]>0.
Let kappa=R(t_0)<1. Then p_j<=p_0 kappa^j. Since t_j^2(3+t_j)/(1-t_j)>=3t_j^2,
t_j<=sqrt(p_0/3) kappa^(j/2).
Consequently the sum of the t_j is at most sqrt(p_0/3)/(1-sqrt(kappa)), and
r_0 2^j<=r_j
=r_0 2^j product_{i=0}^{j-1}(1+t_i/2)
<=r_0 2^j exp(sqrt(p_0/3)/(2(1-sqrt(kappa)))).
Thus s_j=Theta(n_j), with constants depending only on the fixed seed. This establishes exact failure of silver-exponent amplification for every positive-deficit seed under this specified rule.

4. True objective behavior and comparison with the actual benchmark.
The Huber construction proved in fact_id 0be8b54e0a33381c, proof part 1, applies to every nonnegative schedule and gives W_{n_j}(h^(j))>=1/(2s_j+1). Thus the schedules have a lower bound of order 1/n_j.
They also have an upper bound of order 1/n_j from their certificate. Indeed let beta_j=(1+sqrt(1+4C_j))/2. Cancelling the x_star terms in V_h(C)>=0 gives
||x_0-x_star||^2/2+sum_i h_i Q_{i,star}-s(f_n-f_star)
>=||x_n-x_star||^2/2+C||g_n||^2/2.
Add beta Q_{n,star}-beta(f_n-f_star) and use beta^2=C+beta. The right side becomes ||x_n-x_star-beta g_n||^2/2. Since all Q_{i,star}<=0 and all their coefficients are nonnegative,
W_n(h)<=1/(s+beta).
As beta_j>=1, the upper and lower bounds together give W_{n_j}(h^(j))=Theta(1/n_j).

For an explicit comparison with the exact DP benchmark, set lambda=1+sqrt(2) and rho=log_2(lambda). The primitive DP in fact 0be8b54e0a33381c has shifted join
F(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt(A^2+6AB+B^2))/2, so F(A,A)=lambda A. Its primitive sums are nondecreasing because appending the empty primitive block adds phi(x,0)>=1. Hence S_circle(2^k-1)>=lambda^k-1 by induction. For any n>=1 choose k with 2^k<=n<2^{k+1}. The dominant recurrence at split n-1, with empty terminal block, gives S_bullet(n)>=S_circle(n-1). It follows that
B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1>=2lambda^k-1>=2 n^rho/lambda-1.
Therefore the ratio W_{n_j}(h^(j))/U_{n_j}^ZJ grows at least as a positive constant times n_j^(rho-1) and tends to infinity. This is a failure of the specified scalar-potential amplification route, not a universal lower bound and not an impossibility statement about other richer potentials.

author: max3
claim:
Exact single-cut Huber lower bounds are asymptotically insufficient for the Zhang–Jiang profile.

For any integer n>=0 and h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}) in [0,infinity)^n, let W_n(h) be the supremum of 2(f(x_n)-f_star)/(L||x_0-x_star||^2) over all finite-dimensional convex differentiable functions f with L-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer x_star, all x_0!=x_star, and GD x_{t+1}=x_t-(h_t/L)grad f(x_t). Here L>0 is fixed and f_star=f(x_star). Put s(h)=sum_{t=0}^{n-1}h_t. For 0<=j<n let P_j=sum_{t<j}h_t and T_j=sum_{t>j}h_t, and let (u)_+=max(u,0). Define
K_n(h)=max{1/(1+2s(h)), max_{0<=j<n} (h_j-1)_+^2/[(1+P_j)^2(1+2T_j)]},
where the inner maximum is omitted at n=0.
Then W_n(h)>=K_n(h) for every such schedule. Every nonzero term indexed by j is attained as the normalized error of an explicit one-dimensional convex L-smooth instance with a minimizer.

For x,y>=0 define
phi(x,y)=(-x-y+sqrt((x+y+2)^2+4(x+1)(y+1)))/2,
psi(x,y)=(3-2y+sqrt((2y+1)(2y+8x+9)))/4.
Define S_circle(0)=S_bullet(0)=0 and, for n>=1,
S_circle(n)=max_{0<=k<n}[S_circle(k)+phi(S_circle(k),S_circle(n-k-1))+S_circle(n-k-1)],
S_bullet(n)=max_{0<=k<n}[S_circle(k)+psi(S_circle(k),S_bullet(n-k-1))+S_bullet(n-k-1)].
Put B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1, U_n^ZJ=1/B_n, and p=log_2 3.
For all n>=0, S_circle(n)+1<=(n+1)^p and B_n<=1+4n^p.
For every integer n>=2, the schedule ell^(n)_t=t+1, 0<=t<n, satisfies
K_n(ell^(n))<=16/n^2 and
K_n(ell^(n))/U_n^ZJ<=16(1+4n^p)/n^2 -> 0 as n->infinity.
Consequently this particular maximum of the global Huber witness and all these single-cut witnesses cannot itself yield a uniform asymptotic lower bound (1-o(1))U_n^ZJ. This is only a limitation of K_n; it makes no small-error assertion about W_n(ell^(n)) and does not resolve the unrestricted minimax target.
evidence:
## Legal single-cut witness

Scaling permits L=1. Fix j with b=h_j>1; put P=P_j,T=T_j,
c=1/(P+1), a=c(b-1)/(2T+1). Define f(0)=0 and
f'(x)=max(-a,min(c,x)). This derivative is continuous, nondecreasing, and
1-Lipschitz. Hence f is differentiable, convex, 1-smooth, and minimized at0.
Start at x_0=1. Up to the checkpoint all gradients equal c: nonnegative steps
give x_i=1-c sum_{t<i}h_t>=1-cP=c for i<=j. Thus x_j=c, and the checkpoint
sends x_{j+1}=c(1-b)=-a(2T+1).

On the suffix all gradients equal -a. Every suffix partial sum is at most T,
so each iterate is at most -a(2T+1)+aT=-a(T+1)<=-a. Therefore
x_n=-a(T+1), f(x_n)=a^2(T+1/2), and

\[
2f(x_n)=a^2(2T+1)=\frac{(b-1)^2}{(P+1)^2(2T+1)}.
\]

The initial squared distance is1. Multiplying f by L proves the same normalized
statement for every L>0. Terms with h_j<=1 are zero and require no construction.
The global Huber term is proved in predecessor fact 0be8b54e0a33381c, proof
part 1, including zero and empty schedules. Taking a finite maximum preserves
the lower bound, because the worst-case function may depend on h and j.

## A crude exact-recursion bound sufficient for the separation

Set p=log_2 3, C_n=S_circle(n)+1 and B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1.
The primitive recurrence becomes

\[
C_n=\max_{0\leq k<n}\Omega(C_k,C_{n-k-1}),\qquad
\Omega(a,b)=\frac{a+b+\sqrt{(a+b)^2+4ab}}2.
\]

The function Omega is increasing in both nonnegative arguments. When a>=b>=0,
the inequality sqrt((a+b)^2+4ab)<=a+3b follows by squaring, with the right
square exceeding the left by8b^2. Thus Omega(a,b)<=a+2b.
For real u>=v>0, put r=u/v>=1. The derivative of
(r+1)^p-r^p is p[(r+1)^(p-1)-r^(p-1)]>0, so
(r+1)^p-r^p>=2^p-1=2. Consequently
Omega(u^p,v^p)<=u^p+2v^p<=(u+v)^p.
Symmetry handles v>=u. Since C_0=1, induction on n using
u=k+1, v=n-k proves C_n<=(n+1)^p.

The dominant mass recurrence, obtained directly from psi and also displayed
in predecessor 0be8b54e0a33381c, is

\[
B_n=\max_{0\leq k<n}G(C_k,B_{n-k-1}),\qquad
G(a,d)=2a+\frac d2+\frac12\sqrt{d^2+8ad}.
\]

Since sqrt(d^2+8ad)<=d+4a for nonnegative a,d, G(a,d)<=d+4a.
Starting with B_0=1, induction and the primitive bound give, for m=n-k-1,

\[
G(C_k,B_m)\leq1+4m^p+4(k+1)^p\leq1+4n^p.
\]

The last inequality uses u^p+v^p<=(u+v)^p for p>=1 and nonnegative u,v;
this follows, when v>0, by the increasing function (r+1)^p-r^p being at
least its value1 at r=0, and is equality when v=0. Hence B_n<=1+4n^p.

## Linear schedule defeats the single-cut functional

For h_t=t+1, the total sum is n(n+1)/2, so the global Huber term is at most
1/n^2. At checkpoint j, P_j=j(j+1)/2 and (h_j-1)_+=j.
When j>=n/2,

\[
\frac{j^2}{(1+P_j)^2(1+2T_j)}
\leq\frac{4}{j^2}\leq\frac{16}{n^2}.
\]

When j<n/2, the integers satisfy j+1<=(n+1)/2 and j+2<=(n+3)/2. Thus

\[
1+2T_j=1+n(n+1)-(j+1)(j+2)\geq(3n^2+1)/4\geq n^2/2.
\]

Also 1+P_j>=j, so this cut term is at most2/n^2. This includes j=0,
where the numerator is zero. Combining the cases gives K_n<=16/n^2.
Because U_n^ZJ=1/B_n, the ratio is at most16(1+4n^p)/n^2 and tends to0.
All estimates are analytic and valid for every integer n>=2.

The schedules ell^(n) are only counterexamples to the strength of K_n. No
small upper bound on their actual W_n is asserted; they may be very unstable.

author: max
claim: Anticorrelated Markov polytope: an explicit legal persistent-error construction for every constant H>=2, together with an exact (2,3) obstruction to the variable-step local update.
evidence:
UNVERIFIED SUPPORT CONSTRUCTION, not a fact. Fix integer n>=1 and H>=2, put r=-1/(H-1). In R^{n+1} choose an orthonormal basis e_0,...,e_n and define v_0=e_0, v_{i+1}=r v_i+sqrt(1-r^2)e_{i+1}. Then ||v_i||=1 and <v_i,v_j>=r^{|i-j|}. Put x_0=e_0, x_i=e_0-H sum_{t<i}v_t, K=conv(0,v_0,...,v_n), and f_K(x)=max_{u in K}(<x,u>-||u||^2/2). This is a concrete finite-dimensional candidate, with 0 a minimizer and initial distance1.

For completeness, projection characterization establishes global smoothness: the unique maximizer is u=Pi_K(x), by completing the square. The inequalities <x-u,v-u><=0 and <y-v,u-v><=0 for u=Pi_K(x),v=Pi_K(y) imply ||u-v||^2<=<x-y,u-v>, so the projection is1-Lipschitz. Comparing the two maxima gives 0<=f_K(y)-f_K(x)-<u,y-x><=<v-u,y-x><=||y-x||^2, proving differentiability with gradient u. Convexity follows from the maximum of affine functions of x, and f_K>=0, f_K(0)=0 since 0 belongs to K.

Since Hr/(1-r)=-1, geometric sums give <x_i-v_i,v_j>=0 for j>=i, and <x_i-v_i,v_j>=(H-2)(r^{i-j}-1)<=0 for j<i. Also <x_i-v_i,v_i>=0. These inequalities check every vertex of K, including0, and imply <x_i-v_i,u-v_i><=0 for all u in K. Thus Pi_K(x_i)=v_i, the entire GD recursion is legal, and f_K(x_i)=<x_i,v_i>-||v_i||^2/2=1/2. Its normalized terminal error is exactly1 for every n. Randomly rotating K and x_0 gives a distribution of legal instances with the same error1; the random construction of the covariance is a way to specify the geometry, not an extra lower-bound gain.

The naive variable-step mutation r_i=-1/(h_i-1), v_{i+1}=r_i v_i+sqrt(1-r_i^2)e_{i+1} for h_i>=2 is NOT valid in general. Take h=(2,3). Then v_0=(1,0),v_1=(-1,0),v_2=(1/2,sqrt(3)/2), x_0=(1,0),x_1=(-1,0),x_2=(2,0). Every local PSD innovation variance is nonnegative, ||v_i||=1, and <x_i,v_i>=1. But <x_2-v_2,v_0-v_2>=3/2>0, so the old supporting vertex invalidates projection. In fact no convex 1-smooth function minimized at0 realizes the data: optimum interpolation forces f_i-f(0)=1/2 for all i, whereas the pair (x_2,v_2),(x_0,v_0) requires f_2-f_0>=<v_0,x_2-x_0>+||v_2-v_0||^2/2=3/2. Thus this specific local Markov rule fails a nonadjacent interpolation test. The calculation is self-contained; the related support-function/Moreau construction was read in arXiv:2609.09152v2 Section3.1 and AppendixA.2.

author: max3
claim: Explicit ordered Chebyshev schedules defeat the combined witness class of ALL convex quadratics plus the global and every single-cut asymmetric-Huber bound: J_n(h^(n))/U_n^ZJ tends to0.
evidence:
# An explicit ordering defeating quadratics plus all single-cut Huber witnesses

Status: complete candidate derivation, unverified. The initial-wave verification
allowance is already used by fact b98bb807d514e80d. This strengthening is for
main-agent prioritization. Worker: max3.

## Statement and scope

Let K_n(h) be the verified single-cut functional in fact b98bb807d514e80d.
For a schedule h define its exact quadratic-class worst case

\[
Q_n(h)=\max_{0\leq\lambda\leq1}
\lambda\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}(1-h_t\lambda)^2,
\qquad J_n(h)=\max\{K_n(h),Q_n(h)\}.
\]

Here Q_n is exactly the normalized worst case over convex quadratics in any
finite dimension with gradient Lipschitz constant at most L, after scaling
L=1. Indeed diagonalizing their symmetric Hessian makes the normalized error
a weighted average of the displayed scalar expression, and each scalar value
is attained by a one-dimensional quadratic. Thus J_n(h)<=W_n(h).

For every integer n>=3 put theta=pi/(2n+1) and

\[
a_k=\frac1{\sin^2(k\theta)}\quad(1\leq k\leq n).
\]

Define h^(n) by listing a_k with even indices k in decreasing index order,
followed by a_k with odd indices k in increasing index order. For example the
index order at n=7 is (6,4,2,1,3,5,7). This is a fully explicit positive,
finite, predetermined schedule. Then

\[
Q_n(h^{(n)})=\frac1{(2n+1)^2},\qquad
K_n(h^{(n)})\leq72\sin^2\theta
\leq\frac{72\pi^2}{(2n+1)^2}.
\]

Using B_n=1/U_n^ZJ<=1+4n^p with p=log_2 3<2 from verified fact
b98bb807d514e80d, it follows that

\[
\frac{J_n(h^{(n)})}{U_n^{ZJ}}
\leq\frac{72\pi^2(1+4n^p)}{(2n+1)^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]

This rules out proving the target by taking only the maximum of all quadratic
witnesses, the global Huber witness, and the single-cut witnesses in K_n.
It does not give any upper bound on W_n(h^(n)); a nonlinear history-dependent
witness could yield a much larger error.

## Exact quadratic calculation

Define polynomials T_0(x)=1, T_1(x)=x and
T_{r+1}(x)=2xT_r(x)-T_{r-1}(x) for integers r>=1. The cosine addition formula
and induction give T_r(cos u)=cos(ru). The recurrence also shows that T_r
has degree r and parity r. Write M=2n+1. Then T_M is odd and
T_M'(0)=M sin(M pi/2)=(-1)^n M, by differentiating the cosine identity
on -1<x<1. Therefore

\[
R_n(\lambda)=\frac{(-1)^nT_M(\sqrt\lambda)}{M\sqrt\lambda}
\]

extends to a polynomial of degree n with R_n(0)=1. For each k=1,...,n,
T_M(sin(k theta))=cos(M pi/2-k pi)=0. These give n distinct positive
roots of R_n, hence

\[
R_n(\lambda)=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac\lambda{\sin^2(k\theta)}\right).
\]

For lambda in [0,1], |T_M(sqrt(lambda))|<=1. It follows that
lambda R_n(lambda)^2<=1/M^2. At lambda=1, T_M(1)=1 and equality holds.
Permutation of the step factors leaves the product unchanged, proving Q_n.

## Bounds on neighboring step sizes in the stated ordering

All a_k are at least1 and decrease with k. The function sin u/u decreases
on 0<u<=pi/2, since its derivative has numerator u cos u-sin u and the
derivative of that numerator is -u sin u<=0. Hence whenever k+2<=n,

\[
\frac{a_k}{a_{k+2}}
=\frac{\sin^2((k+2)\theta)}{\sin^2(k\theta)}
\leq\left(\frac{k+2}{k}\right)^2.
\tag{1}
\]

The first even-indexed step and the last odd-indexed step have index at
least n-1. Since n>=3 implies (n-1)/(2n+1)>=1/4, both are at most2.
Also a_2>=a_1/4 and a_3>=a_1/9, by the same decreasing-sinc argument
(or the double-angle identity for a_2).

## Every single-cut term remains small

For a selected position j, write b=h_j, P=P_j, T=T_j as in the verified
definition of K_n. Replace (b-1)_+ by b when an upper estimate is needed.

1. A step before the central largest step a_1 has even index. If it is the
first step, b/(P+1)<=2. Otherwise its preceding step is a_{k+2}; by (1),
b<=4a_{k+2}<=4P. Thus b/(P+1)<=4 in either case. Its suffix contains a_1,
so its cut term is at most16/(1+2a_1)<=8/a_1.

2. At a_1 the prefix contains a_2>=a_1/4 and the suffix contains
a_3>=a_1/9. Therefore its cut term is at most

\[
\frac{a_1^2}{(a_1/4)^2(2a_1/9)}=\frac{72}{a_1}.
\]

3. After a_1, the prefix always has P>=a_1. For a step a_k that is not
the last step, k is odd and k>=3, and its suffix contains a_{k+2}.
By (1), a_{k+2}>=a_k/4. Its cut term is at most

\[
\frac{a_k^2}{a_1^2(2a_k/4)}
=\frac{2a_k}{a_1^2}\leq\frac2{a_1}.
\]

At the last step b<=2, hence (b-1)^2<=1 and the cut term is at most
1/a_1^2<=1/a_1.

Finally the global Huber term is at most1/(1+2a_1)<=1/(2a_1).
The maximum of these bounds is72/a_1=72 sin^2 theta. Since sin(theta)<=theta,
this proves the claimed estimate, entirely analytically for every n>=3.

## Source grounding

The standard trigonometric definition of T_r is documented at NIST DLMF
18.5.1, https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.5. The polynomial identities used here are
derived above from their recurrence, so no external theorem is used as a
black-box proof step. Matlas was queried for the weighted Chebyshev product
identity and did not return a useful exact hit.

author: max4
claim: Cross-term fusion screen, beyond the earlier scalar-deficit rule: (i) the rational motif [3/2,3/2] has an exact saturated primitive certificate with nonlocal interpolation multipliers, proving that cross terms can repair scalar deficits; (ii) nevertheless pairing any known ZJ objective block of length n with its reverse cannot improve the primitive DP capacity at length 2n, because S_circle(2n)+1>2S_bullet(n)+1 for n>=1; (iii) an explicit asymmetric two-bridge rule promising a larger three-block capacity fails already on the primitive block [sqrt(2)] by a legal one-dimensional Huber example. These are unverified route-screening findings, not target results.
evidence:
Notation. Put P_n=S_circle(n)+1 and B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1, with exact DP definitions and normalized worst-case W_n as in fact 0be8b54e0a33381c. Define homogeneous scalar joins
F(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt(A^2+6AB+B^2))/2,
G(A,D)=2A+D/2+sqrt(D^2+8AD)/2
for positive A,B,D. The exact recurrences are
P_0=B_0=1,
P_n=max_{k+l+1=n} F(P_k,P_l),
B_n=max_{k+l+1=n} G(P_k,B_l).

1. A real cross-term repair, with no bridge.
For a nonnegative schedule h of length n and sum s, define the intrinsic potential
V_h(C)=2 sum_{i<n} h_i(f_i-f_n)+sum_{i<n}h_i(1-h_i)||g_i||^2-C||g_n||^2.
This is the same potential as in candidate 79da55e26c4a7406: the cross terms from the GD displacement cancel exactly.
Let Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2<=0 for convex 1-smooth functions, with x_{i+1}=x_i-h_i g_i.
For h=[3/2,3/2], s=3 and C=s(s+1)=12, the following formal identity holds:
V_h(12)=(7/2)(-Q_10)+(-Q_01)+14(-Q_21)+(17/2)(-Q_12)+(-Q_20)+(1/2)(-Q_02).
All six multipliers are nonnegative. To check it, put u=g_0,v=g_1,w=g_2, x_1=x_0-(3/2)u and x_2=x_1-(3/2)v. Function coefficients become 3(f_0-f_1)+6(f_1-f_2); squared-gradient coefficients become -3||u||^2/4-3||v||^2/4-12||w||^2; and all three cross coefficients cancel. This is precisely V_h(12).
Thus a bridge-free two-block proof with retained history inequalities repairs the deficit of the one-step [3/2] seed. It is a concrete demonstration that the scalar-deficit obstruction does not forbid richer fusion. However its mass is 4, below P_2=F(1,1+sqrt(2)), so this test seed is not an improvement.

2. Exact capacity screen for pairing ZJ objective schedules with their reversals.
We prove the scalar inequality
F(A,F(D,A))>G(A,D) for A,D>0.
By homogeneity set A=1 and d=D/A. Let q=F(1,d), z=F(1,q), g=G(1,d). The defining quadratic identities give
d=q(q-1)/(q+1), q=z(z-1)/(z+1),
so d=z(z-1)(z^2-2z-1)/[(z+1)(z^2+1)] and z>1+sqrt(2)>2.
The larger root g>2 satisfies d=g-4+4/g. Direct expansion yields
(z-4+4/z)-d=4/[z(z+1)(z^2+1)]>0.
The function t maps to t-4+4/t is strictly increasing for t>2, since its derivative is 1-4/t^2>0. Hence z>g and the displayed inequality follows after restoring A.

We now prove P_{2n}>=B_n for every n>=0, strictly for n>=1. At n=0 both equal 1. For n>=1 choose a maximizing split k+l+1=n for B_n. By induction P_{2l}>=B_l. The primitive DP permits the two joins
P_{2n}>=F(P_k,F(P_{2l},P_k))
>=F(P_k,F(B_l,P_k))
>G(P_k,B_l)=B_n.
All indices are valid: the inner length is 2l+k+1 and the outer length is 2l+2k+2=2n. This is a pure algebraic property of the actual DP, not an assertion of unrestricted schedule optimality.

If h is a ZJ objective schedule of length n and sum S_bullet(n), the concatenated schedule [h,reverse(h)] has length 2n and shifted sum 2S_bullet(n)+1=B_n. Even if a new richer proof established that this concatenation is primitive, its capacity would still be strictly below P_{2n}, so every subsequent ordinary ConPP/ConPD construction using it can replace it by the existing same-length primitive DP block with a greater scalar capacity. Thus this fusion route using only existing ZJ objective blocks cannot furnish the requested strict improvement. General f/g-to-primitive closure was not assumed or claimed.
A nonbasic f/g seed of length n would need shifted pair mass strictly larger than P_{2n} even to escape this exact capacity screen, and then would still need a valid primitive certificate.

3. A hostile test of a different, direct three-block join.
Choose exact constants c=1/4 and d=(-5+5sqrt(17))/8-1=(5sqrt(17)-13)/8. Then 0<d<1 and
c d (3+c+d)=1.
Let M=3+c+d. A tempting homogeneous triple-primitive rule, on a primitive block a of shifted sum A=1+s(a), is
J(a)=[a, 1+cA, a, 1+dA, a].
Its shifted sum is M A. Because c d M=1, it balances the full-curvature quadratic endpoint product when the seed block has product 1/A; M exceeds the ordinary two-join factor F(1,F(1,1)) (numerically M is about 4.20194, versus about 4.01545). Quadratic/Huber balance alone therefore makes it an attractive but insufficient candidate.

It is not a universally primitive join. Take the exact primitive one-step block a=[sqrt(2)], write A=1+sqrt(2), and let
P=2sqrt(2)+1+cA
be the sum of all steps before the larger bridge b=1+dA. The tail is the one step sqrt(2). Define the convex 1-smooth function
f(x)=x^2/2 for x<=1,
f(x)=x-1/2 for x>=1,
with minimizer 0. Its derivative is min(x,1), continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz.
Start at x_0=P+1=(2+c)A. Every step before b occurs with derivative 1 and the point immediately before b is 1. The bridge sends it to -dA. The final sqrt(2) step is taken in the quadratic region and yields
x_final=(sqrt(2)-1)dA=d,
which lies in (0,1). At every trajectory point, Q_{i,star}=f_i-<g_i,x_i>+||g_i||^2/2=0: the identity holds in both pieces of this explicit function.
For a saturated primitive schedule of shifted sum R=1+s, its potential would require x_0^2>=R^2 x_final^2 whenever the final point is in the quadratic piece and all Q_{i,star}=0. Here R=M A, so it would require
(2+c)^2 A^2 >= M^2 A^2 d^2.
But Md=1/c=4, whereas 2+c=9/4; the inequality is strictly false. Hence the proposed primitive interface is refuted exactly, in dimension one.
This hostile test rules out that uniform join rule; it does not exclude a horizon-dependent rule valid only for a different restricted block family. Any such reopening must supply a new certificate and re-test the full smooth-convex class.

author: max2
claim:
Complex-polynomial transcripts, an explicit legal spectral lens, and a quantitative limit of that lens.

For each integer n>=1 and each real nonnegative schedule h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}), define Poly_0(z)=1 and Poly_i(z)=product_{t=0}^{i-1}(1-h_t z) for 1<=i<=n. Identify the complex plane with the real Euclidean plane, with inner product <u,v>=Re(conj(u)v). For z=alpha+i beta set xi_i=Poly_i(z), gamma_i=z Poly_i(z) for 0<=i<=n, and xi_*=gamma_*=0. Put kappa=alpha-|z|^2 and I_n={*,0,...,n}. For each ordered pair define
q_ij=<gamma_j,xi_i-xi_j>+||gamma_i-gamma_j||^2/2,
regarded as the weight on the directed edge j->i. For each directed simple cycle C in I_n define
Area_C=sum_{j->i in C} Im(conj(xi_j)xi_i),
Energy_C=sum_{j->i in C}|xi_i-xi_j|^2.
Define D_h to be the set of z satisfying kappa Energy_C>=2|beta Area_C| for every such cycle.

(a) The data (xi_i,gamma_i), including the optimum sample *, are interpolable by a finite everywhere-defined convex differentiable function f:R^2->R with 1-Lipschitz gradient and grad f(0)=0 if and only if z belongs to D_h. For z in D_h let ell_i be the largest q-weight of a directed path i->*, allowing the empty path at *, and put v_i=-ell_i. The maxima exist over simple paths and ell_*=0. There is such an f with f(xi_i)=v_i for every i. These values are simultaneously maximal among all interpolating f satisfying f(0)=0. Its exact GD recursion for h starts at xi_0=1, and its normalized terminal error is
Gap_h(z):=-2ell_n.
In particular
|z|^2|Poly_n(z)|^2 <= Gap_h(z) <= (2alpha-|z|^2)|Poly_n(z)|^2.

(b) The parameter lens
Lens_n={alpha+i beta: alpha-alpha^2-beta^2>=|beta|cot(pi/(n+2))}
is contained in D_h for every h.

(c) Let T_j be the polynomials defined by T_0(x)=1, T_1(x)=x and T_{j+1}(x)=2xT_j(x)-T_{j-1}(x). For every n>=2 define the positive schedule Chi_n, in any permutation, by the n entries
sec^2((2k-1)pi/(2(2n+1))), k=1,...,n.
Its terminal polynomial is (-1)^n T_{2n+1}(sqrt(z))/((2n+1)sqrt(z)), interpreted as a polynomial including z=0, and its sum is s(Chi_n)=2n(n+1)/3. For all z in Lens_n,
Gap_{Chi_n}(z) <= 2cosh^2(2)/(2n+1)^2.

For an arbitrary schedule of length n>=1 define
V_lens(h)=max{sup_{z in Lens_n} Gap_h(z), 1/(2s(h)+1)}.
Let W_n(h) be the project worst-case normalized objective error, namely the supremum of 2(f(x_n)-f_star)/(L||x_0-x_star||^2) over every finite dimension, convex differentiable f with L-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer x_star, and x_0!=x_star, using x_{t+1}=x_t-(h_t/L)grad f(x_t). Here L>0 is fixed and s(h)=sum h_t. Then V_lens(h)<=W_n(h). For the exact benchmark U_n^ZJ=1/(2S_bullet(n)+1) defined by the recursions in predecessor b98bb807d514e80d, and p=log_2 3 from that predecessor, the explicit schedules satisfy
0<=V_lens(Chi_n)/U_n^ZJ
 <= 2cosh^2(2)(1+4n^p)/n^2 ->0.
Thus the universal-lens witnesses, even augmented by the canonical sum-based Huber witness, cannot prove the required uniform matching lower bound. This is a limitation of that witness family only, not an upper bound on W_n(Chi_n) and not a decision of the unrestricted minimax target.
evidence:
1. Necessary smooth-convex inequality.
For any convex differentiable 1-smooth f and any x,y, put k(u)=f(u)-<grad f(y),u>. Convexity and grad k(y)=0 imply k(y)<=k(u). Integrating the Lipschitz gradient along a segment gives k(u+d)<=k(u)+<grad k(u),d>+||d||^2/2. Take d=-grad k(u) and combine these inequalities to obtain
f(x)>=f(y)+<grad f(y),x-y>+||grad f(x)-grad f(y)||^2/2. (1)
Applied to any proposed interpolant, (1) says its values obey f_i-f_j>=q_ij.

2. Cycle identity and necessity.
For complex u,v, <u,v>=Re(conj(u)v). Expand
<z xi_j,xi_i-xi_j>
=alpha Re(conj(xi_j)(xi_i-xi_j))+beta Im(conj(xi_j)xi_i).
The real part is (|xi_i|^2-|xi_j|^2-|xi_i-xi_j|^2)/2. Also
||gamma_i-gamma_j||^2=|z|^2|xi_i-xi_j|^2.
Therefore
q_ij=(alpha/2)(|xi_i|^2-|xi_j|^2)+beta Im(conj(xi_j)xi_i)
      -(kappa/2)|xi_i-xi_j|^2. (2)
The norm-difference terms telescope on a cycle, whose weight is beta Area_C-kappa Energy_C/2. Both orientations are available, and their areas have opposite signs but equal energies. Consequently nonpositivity of every cycle is equivalent to the definition of D_h. Summing (1) on cycles proves the necessary implication in (a). The cycle *->0->* also forces kappa>=0.

3. Values from paths.
Assume z is in D_h. Every closed walk is a sum of simple directed cycles, after splitting at repeated vertices; thus every closed walk has nonpositive weight. Any path to * can have repeated vertices deleted, and deleting the intervening nonpositive cycle cannot reduce the weight. There are finitely many simple paths on I_n, so ell_i is finite and is a maximum over them. At * the empty path has weight zero and every closed walk has weight at most zero, so ell_*=0.
Concatenate edge j->i with a maximum path i->*, then delete cycles if needed. It follows that ell_j>=q_ij+ell_i. Hence v_i=-ell_i satisfies v_i-v_j>=q_ij. For any other feasible values F_i with F_*=0, summing the inequalities along a path i->* yields -F_i at least the weight of that path. Thus F_i<=-ell_i=v_i for every i.

4. A finite-dimensional global interpolant.
Define on the real plane
H(g)=max_{i in I_n}{<gamma_i,xi_i>-v_i+<xi_i,g-gamma_i>+||g-gamma_i||^2/2}.
This is the maximum of finitely many quadratics with Hessian equal to the identity. It is finite, continuous and 1-strongly convex. The inequality v_j-v_i>=<gamma_i,xi_j-xi_i>+||gamma_j-gamma_i||^2/2 is exactly the assertion that at g=gamma_i the j-th quadratic is at most the i-th quadratic. Thus
H(gamma_i)=<gamma_i,xi_i>-v_i.
The i-th quadratic is active and has derivative xi_i at gamma_i. Its supporting affine function is below H, so xi_i belongs to the subdifferential of H at gamma_i.

Define f(x)=sup_g{<x,g>-H(g)}. For each fixed x, the maximizer g(x) exists and is unique: H(g)-<x,g> is continuous, strongly convex, and coercive because even any one term of the defining maximum has leading term ||g||^2/2. Optimality says x belongs to the subdifferential of H at g(x). Strong convexity implies that for all x,y,
<x-y,g(x)-g(y)>>=||g(x)-g(y)||^2.
To justify this implication, subtract ||g||^2/2 from H, write the two supporting-subgradient inequalities at g(x),g(y), and add them. Cauchy--Schwarz gives ||g(x)-g(y)||<=||x-y||.
The definition of f yields, for every displacement d,
<g(x),d><=f(x+d)-f(x)<=<g(x+d),d>.
It follows that the difference between f(x+d)-f(x) and <g(x),d> lies in [0,||d||^2]. Therefore f is differentiable with gradient g(x), and that gradient is 1-Lipschitz. It is finite by existence of the maximizers and convex as a supremum of affine functions. The subgradient condition xi_i in partial H(gamma_i) gives g(xi_i)=gamma_i and f(xi_i)=v_i. At the optimum sample this gives f(0)=0 and grad f(0)=0, so convexity makes 0 a minimizer.

The prefix-polynomial identity Poly_{i+1}=(1-h_i z)Poly_i gives xi_{i+1}=xi_i-h_i gamma_i. Thus the interpolation is a legal GD trajectory, with ||xi_0||=1. Apply (1) in both directions between n and *:
v_n>=||gamma_n||^2/2,
v_n<=<gamma_n,xi_n>-||gamma_n||^2/2.
Since <gamma_n,xi_n>=alpha|Poly_n(z)|^2, these are the two bounds in (a).

5. A discrete area-energy inequality.
Consider any r>=2 complex numbers w_0,...,w_{r-1}, with w_r=w_0. Put
d_k=(1/r)sum_{j=0}^{r-1}w_j exp(-2pi i k j/r), 0<=k<r.
The finite geometric-sum identity reconstructs w_j=sum_k d_k exp(2pi i k j/r). The same identity, on expanding the quadratic sums, gives
sum_j Im(conj(w_j)w_{j+1})=r sum_k |d_k|^2 sin(2pi k/r),
sum_j |w_{j+1}-w_j|^2=4r sum_k |d_k|^2 sin^2(pi k/r).
The k=0 terms vanish. For 1<=k<r, the ratio of the absolute sine coefficient in the first sum to the coefficient in the second is (1/2)|cot(pi k/r)|<=cot(pi/r)/2. The triangle inequality proves
|sum_j Im(conj(w_j)w_{j+1})| <= (cot(pi/r)/2)sum_j |w_{j+1}-w_j|^2. (3)
This also covers r=2, where the left side and cot(pi/2) are zero.
Every simple cycle on I_n has length r<=n+2. The function cot(pi/r) increases as the integer r>=2 increases. From (3) and the defining inequality for Lens_n one gets kappa Energy_C>=2|beta Area_C|. This proves (b).

6. Explicit real positive Chebyshev steps and their sum.
The recurrence for T_j, the cosine addition formula, and induction give T_j(cos t)=cos(jt). Its parity is the parity of j and its degree is j. Put m=2n+1. The odd polynomial T_m(x) is divisible by x; hence (-1)^n T_m(sqrt(z))/(m sqrt(z)) is a real polynomial of degree n. Differentiating T_m(cos t)=cos(mt) at t=pi/2 gives T_m'(0)=(-1)^n m, so its value at z=0 is 1.
The positive roots of T_m are cos((2k-1)pi/(2m)), k=1,...,n. Squaring them gives exactly the distinct roots lambda_k=cos^2((2k-1)pi/(2m)) in (0,1) of the degree-n polynomial. It follows from the value at zero that the polynomial equals product_k(1-z/lambda_k). Thus its reciprocal roots are precisely the stated positive schedule, regardless of their order.

Twice differentiating the cosine identity and eliminating the angle gives the polynomial identity
(1-x^2)T_m''(x)-xT_m'(x)+m^2 T_m(x)=0.
Differentiation at x=0 gives T_m'''(0)=-(m^2-1)T_m'(0). The coefficient of z in (-1)^n T_m(sqrt(z))/(m sqrt(z)) is consequently -(m^2-1)/6. The coefficient of z in the product of schedule factors is minus their sum. Hence s(Chi_n)=(m^2-1)/6=2n(n+1)/3.

7. The lens lies in an ellipse of small width.
Let n>=2, N=n+2, theta=pi/N, t=tan(theta)>0, and u=asinh(t/2)>0. For z=alpha+i beta in Lens_n,
0<=alpha<=1 and |beta|<=t alpha(1-alpha),
because alpha-alpha^2-beta^2>=0 and dropping beta^2 only weakens the defining inequality. Put s=alpha(1-alpha), so 0<=s<=1/4. Since sinh(u)=t/2 and cosh(u)>=1,
(2alpha-1)^2/cosh^2(u)+(2beta)^2/sinh^2(u)
 <=1-4s+16s^2<=1. (4)

For completeness (4) implies there is a complex w with |Im w|<=u and z=(1+cos w)/2. If beta=0, take a real w with cos w=2alpha-1. If beta!=0, the continuous function
v -> (2alpha-1)^2/cosh^2(v)+(2beta)^2/sinh^2(v)
decreases from infinity as v increases from zero and is at most 1 at v=u. Choose v in (0,u] where its value is 1, and choose a real angle a with
cos a=(2alpha-1)/cosh(v), sin a=-2beta/sinh(v).
Then w=a+i v has cos w=2alpha-1+2i beta.
A square root of z is cos(w/2). The cosine identity for T_m holds for complex arguments as well, because it follows from polynomial recurrence and the complex cosine addition formula. Thus
|z| |Poly_n(z)|^2
 =|T_m(sqrt(z))|^2/m^2
 =|cos(mw/2)|^2/m^2
 <=cosh^2(m u/2)/m^2. (5)
The polynomial interpretation covers z=0 as well; both sides of the equality before the bound are zero there.

The inequality asinh(t/2)<=t/2 follows by integrating its derivative, which is at most 1 on the nonnegative line. The function tan is convex on [0,pi/4], so it lies below its chord and tan(theta)<=4theta/pi=4/N. Therefore m u/2<=m t/4<=m/N<2. Combining (5) with (a) and alpha<=|z| proves
Gap_{Chi_n}(z)<=(2alpha-|z|^2)|Poly_n(z)|^2
 <=2|z||Poly_n(z)|^2<=2cosh^2(2)/(2n+1)^2.

8. Canonical Huber witness and the exact-profile comparison.
For any h>=0 let S=s(h) and delta=1/(2S+1). In dimension one define
f_delta(x)=x^2/2 for |x|<=delta, and delta|x|-delta^2/2 otherwise.
The matching derivative is x clipped to [-delta,delta], hence is continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz. The function is convex, differentiable, 1-smooth and minimized at 0. Starting from x_0=1, every partial sum of h lies in [0,S]. Induction gives x_i=1-delta sum_{t<i}h_t>=1-delta S=(S+1)/(2S+1)>=delta. Thus every gradient equals delta and
2f_delta(x_n)=2delta(1-delta S)-delta^2=1/(2S+1).
Multiplying either this function or the interpolant from part 4 by L produces the same normalized error for the specified arbitrary L>0. Consequently each term defining V_lens(h) is a legal lower-bound witness for W_n(h), proving V_lens(h)<=W_n(h).

For Chi_n the Huber term is
1/(1+4n(n+1)/3)<=3/(4n^2).
Part 7 bounds its lens term by 2cosh^2(2)/(2n+1)^2. Since 2cosh^2(2)>=2>3/4, both terms are at most 2cosh^2(2)/n^2.
Verified predecessor b98bb807d514e80d states, for exactly the project phi/psi recursions and the project normalization, that B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1<=1+4n^p with p=log_2 3<2. Multiply the preceding bound on V_lens by B_n to obtain the displayed ratio estimate. It tends to zero because n^{-2}->0 and n^{p-2}->0. This uses no assumed limit for S_bullet(n)/n^rho and no numerical estimate of the profile constant.

Only the explicitly restricted witness family was upper bounded. None of the calculations gives an upper bound for the unrestricted W_n on the displayed schedules.

glossary.Poly_i: Ordered prefix polynomial product_{t<i}(1-h_t z), with Poly_0=1.
glossary.xi_i: Complex prefix point Poly_i(z), identified with a vector of R^2; xi_*=0.
glossary.gamma_i: Complex gradient z Poly_i(z), identified with a vector of R^2; gamma_*=0.
glossary.q_ij: Smooth interpolation lower-increment edge weight on directed edge j->i.
glossary.Area_C: Signed doubled polygon area sum Im(conj(xi_j)xi_i) over a directed cycle.
glossary.Energy_C: Sum of squared edge lengths of that directed cycle.
glossary.D_h: Set of complex parameters satisfying every stated smooth-convex interpolation cycle.
glossary.ell_i: Maximum q-weight over paths i->*, with empty optimum path allowed.
glossary.v_i: Maximal interpolating function value -ell_i with optimum value zero.
glossary.Gap_h: The maximal normalized terminal error -2ell_n for the given complex-polynomial transcript.
glossary.Chi_n: Any ordering of the n positive reciprocal squared Chebyshev roots specified in the statement.
glossary.V_lens: Maximum of the universal complex-lens witness supremum and the canonical sum-based Huber witness.
glossary.T_j: Chebyshev polynomials T_0=1, T_1=x, T_{j+1}=2xT_j-T_{j-1}; local notation in this fact.
glossary.H: The maximum of shifted quadratic functions whose convex conjugate constructs the interpolant.

author: max
claim: P4 screening: exact two-state matrix payoff for random two-curvature quadratics; fixed-one-curvature and fixed finite curvature-support mechanisms fail, while the continuous-profile comparison remains BLOCKED.
evidence:
UNVERIFIED EXACT REALIZATION AND PAYOFF. For a,b in(0,1], let J_{a,b}(x)=a x^2/2 on x>=0 and b x^2/2 on x<=0. Its derivative is a x or b x on the two half-lines, agrees at0, is nondecreasing, and is1-Lipschitz (for x<=0<=y, a y-b x<=y-x). It is convex and differentiable, with minimizer0. Start at x0=+1 or-1 with probability1/2, so the initial squared distance is1 in every sample.

Define a nonnegative two-by-two matrix
N_h(a,b)=[[(1-ha)_+^2,(hb-1)_+^2],[(ha-1)_+^2,(1-hb)_+^2]].
If a column represents the expected squared magnitude currently on its indicated sign, multiplying by this matrix gives the next signed squared-magnitude masses. This holds because the step is x -> (1-ha)x on the positive half-line and x -> (1-hb)x on the negative half-line. A zero iterate contributes zero mass, so the sign convention at0 is irrelevant.
Thus for every predetermined nonnegative schedule h the exact expected normalized objective under this initial-sign law is
P_h(a,b)=(1/2)[a,b] N_{h_{n-1}}(a,b)...N_{h_0}(a,b)[1,1]^T.
For any Borel probability law nu_h on(0,1]^2, selected after the complete schedule is known, the joint law on (a,b,initial sign) consists only of legal normalized instances and yields
W_n(h)>=integral P_h(a,b)dnu_h(a,b).
The integrand is bounded for fixed finite h, since each normalized error is at most product_i(1+h_i)^2. No infimum is moved through expectation. The matrices retain order and state-dependent curvature; at a=b they reduce to the usual quadratic polynomial model.

Direct attack1 refutes the fixed-a=1 subclass as a universal hard family. For h=(1,H,1), H>=1, the positive initial point is killed at the first step. From x0=-1 one has x1=-(1-b). If Hb>=1, the second step reaches the nonnegative half-line and the final unit step kills it. If Hb<=1, x3=-(1-Hb)(1-b)^2. Therefore
P_{(1,H,1)}(1,b)=(b/2)(1-Hb)_+^2(1-b)^4<=2/(27H),
because max_{0<=t<=1}t(1-t)^2=4/27. The supremum over either deterministic initial sign is at most4/(27H). Every distribution over b has the same upper cap and it tends to0 with H at horizon3.

Direct attack2: let Lambda be any fixed finite subset of(0,1]. List its reciprocals in nondecreasing order and use them as the steps. Every objective J_{a,b} with a,b in Lambda is solved exactly from either initial sign. Before the first step equal to the reciprocal of the starting-side curvature, all steps are smaller, so the iterate retains its sign. At that reciprocal step it reaches0 and remains there. Appending zero steps gives exact solution for all larger horizons. Thus a fixed finite support of curvatures cannot furnish the sought all-schedule lower bound.

Neither attack settles the genuinely continuous two-curvature class. The unresolved statement would be: for every epsilon>0 there exists N_epsilon independent of h such that for every n>=N_epsilon and h in[0,infinity)^n there is a probability nu_h on(0,1]^2 with integral P_h dnu_h >=(1-epsilon)U_n^ZJ. Equivalently replace the integral by sup_{a,b} P_h(a,b), since point masses are allowed (no minimax interchange). This is a restricted-family theorem of the full desired lower-bound strength and is currently BLOCKED; the explicit matrix formula alone is not a bridge proving it.

evidence:
# A legal multi-cut construction with exact remote-history transfer

Status: complete candidate derivation, unverified. No second initial-wave
verification submission is made. Worker: max3.

This is an actual one-dimensional convex 1-smooth function construction,
not a free choice of curvature at each iterate and not a PEP reformulation.
It keeps remote ray offsets and function-value areas. It gives a lower-bound
functional stronger than the verified single-cut functional K_n, but no
uniform comparison to U_n^ZJ has been proved.

## Inputs, feasibility, and quantitative output

Take any finite nonnegative schedule and select k checkpoint steps. In
chronological order write the schedule as

\[
(\ell_0,b_0,\ell_1,b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1},\ell_k),
\]

where each ell_i is a possibly empty list of nonnegative ordinary steps,
s_i is its sum, and b_i is a nonnegative checkpoint step. This preserves
the individual steps and their order; their sums suffice only because the
constructed derivative will be constant during each ordinary block.

For k>=1 define nonterminal gradient magnitudes v_0,...,v_{k-1} and
nonnegative offset sums O_0,...,O_k as follows:

\[
v_0=\frac1{1+s_0},\qquad O_0=0,
\]

and, for i=0,...,k-2,

\[
v_{i+1}=\frac{(b_i-1)v_i-O_i}{1+s_{i+1}},\qquad
O_{i+1}=O_i+s_i v_i.
\tag{1}
\]

Also set O_k=O_{k-1}+s_{k-1}v_{k-1}; its last value is only bookkeeping.
Require

\[
v_i>0\quad(0\leq i<k),\qquad
v_i\geq v_{i-2}\quad(2\leq i<k).
\tag{2}
\]

Define the terminal distance budget and earlier terminal-ray slope by

\[
Z=(b_{k-1}-1)v_{k-1}-O_{k-1},\qquad
v_{\rm old}=\begin{cases}0,&k=1,\\v_{k-2},&k\geq2.\end{cases}
\]

The terminal feasibility requirement is

\[
Z\geq(1+s_k)v_{\rm old}.
\tag{3}
\]

Choose any final slope magnitude

\[
q\in\left[v_{\rm old},\frac{Z}{1+s_k}\right].
\tag{4}
\]

Put E=sum of s_i v_i^2 over 0<=i<k with i congruent to k modulo2.
There is a convex differentiable 1-smooth f:R->R with minimizer0 and
f(0)=0 such that GD from x_0=1 with the exact supplied schedule has

\[
2f(x_n)=2E+2qZ-(2s_k+1)q^2.
\tag{5}
\]

Thus this expression is a legal lower bound on W_n(h). Scaling f by L
preserves the normalized statement at any L>0. The best q within (4) is

\[
q_{\rm opt}=\max\left\{v_{\rm old},\frac{Z}{2s_k+1}\right\}.
\tag{6}
\]

Indeed the quadratic in (5) is concave, its unconstrained maximum is at
Z/(2s_k+1), and this point is no larger than the upper endpoint in (4).

For k=0 take Z=1, E=0, v_old=0 and s_k=s_0. Equations (4)--(6) then
give the usual exact Huber value 1/(1+2s_0). For k=1 and b_0>=1, the
terminal old slope is0, and (5)--(6) give exactly
(b_0-1)^2/[(1+s_0)^2(1+2s_1)]. Therefore the maximum over all feasible
selected chains includes every term of K_n in fact b98bb807d514e80d.

## Explicit construction on the two rays

Write a signed point as x=(-1)^i r at stage i, where r>=0 is its distance
from0. On each ray construct a radial derivative magnitude Q_+(r) or Q_-(r),
starting at Q_+(0)=Q_-(0)=0. Let A_+ and A_- denote the largest distances
previously visited on those rays, and let w_+,w_- be their derivative
magnitudes. Initially all four numbers are0.

At a nonterminal stage i the starting distance is a_i. On its active ray
write A_old,w_old for the previous record and slope and d_i=A_old-w_old.
Choose the magnitude v_i and extend that ray's derivative by a slope-1 ramp
from (A_old,w_old) to

\[
(r_i,v_i),\qquad r_i=A_{\rm old}+v_i-w_{\rm old}=d_i+v_i,
\]

followed by a constant segment of value v_i up to a_i. Conditions (2)
give v_i>=w_old; for the first visit to a ray its old slope is0. The
recurrence will give

\[
a_i=d_i+(1+s_i)v_i=r_i+s_i v_i,
\tag{7}
\]

so a_i>=r_i>=A_old. This extension does not change any previously visited
data. During ell_i every iterate remains on this flat segment, since its
partial step sums lie between0 and s_i. Thus the stage ends at signed
distance r_i with gradient sign (-1)^i and magnitude v_i.

At the checkpoint b_i the next signed point has opposite sign and distance

\[
a_{i+1}=b_i v_i-r_i=(b_i-1)v_i-d_i.
\tag{8}
\]

The previously unvisited amount will be nonnegative by the next-stage
feasibility condition. The active ray's new outer record is a_i and its
slope there is v_i. Hence its offset on its next visit is

\[
d_{i+2}=a_i-v_i=d_i+s_i v_i.
\tag{9}
\]

Initially d_0=d_1=0. Write O_i=d_i+d_{i+1}. Equations (8)--(9) imply
O_{i+1}=O_i+s_i v_i and
a_{i+1}-d_{i+1}=(b_i-1)v_i-O_i. Equating this last quantity with
(1+s_{i+1})v_{i+1} gives exactly (1). Also a_0=1 and d_0=0 imply the
stated v_0, completing the induction that verifies (7) for each nonterminal
stage. Positive v_i means nonterminal stages do not reach0. The terminal
case Z=0 is permitted only with zero old slope and causes no difficulty.

At terminal stage k, the starting distance satisfies a_k-d_k=Z. Extend
its ray by a slope-1 ramp from its old record to slope q and then by a flat
segment to a_k. Condition (4) makes the ramp endpoint d_k+q no smaller
than the old record and no larger than a_k-s_k q. Thus every final-block
iterate stays on its flat segment. The final distance is a_k-s_k q.

For k=0 the same construction begins directly from the initial origin datum,
with a_0=1 and q given by (4).

After the last stage extend each radial derivative constantly to infinity.
Define the global derivative by f'(x)=Q_+(x) for x>=0 and
f'(x)=-Q_-(-x) for x<=0, and define f(x)=integral_0^x f'(t)dt.
Each radial derivative is continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz, with
Q_+(0)=Q_-(0)=0. Across0, for x<=0<=y,

\[
0\leq f'(y)-f'(x)=Q_+(y)+Q_-(-x)\leq y-x.
\]

Consequently f' is globally continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz.
This proves differentiability, convexity, 1-smoothness, and a minimizer at0.
The earlier stage calculations prove the exact original GD recursion.
In particular no interpolation or dimensional-realizability gap remains
within the candidate construction.

## Retained function values give the exact objective

On one ray, a ramp from magnitude w to v adds area (v^2-w^2)/2. Its
following nonterminal flat segment has length s_i v_i and adds s_i v_i^2.
Therefore at the outer record after any nonterminal stage i, the radial
function value equals

\[
v_i^2/2+\sum_{j\leq i,\ j\equiv i\ ({\rm mod}\ 2)}s_jv_j^2.
\tag{10}
\]

This identity follows by induction on successive visits to that ray: the
squared-gradient contributions telescope and the flat-segment areas remain.
At the final stage the new ramp endpoint has value E+q^2/2. The distance
from that endpoint to the final point is Z-(s_k+1)q, on which the derivative
equals q. The final value is consequently

\[
E+q^2/2+q[Z-(s_k+1)q]
=E+qZ-(s_k+1/2)q^2,
\]

proving (5). The initial distance is exactly1, so the normalization is exact.

## Exact two-cut illustration

For h=(1,5,1,9,1) select checkpoint steps5 and9. Then s_0=s_1=s_2=1,
v_0=1/2, O_0=0, v_1=1, O_1=1/2, Z=15/2, v_old=1/2,
E=1/4, and q_opt=5/2. All feasibility conditions hold. Formula (5) gives

\[
W_5(1,5,1,9,1)\geq2(1/4)+(15/2)^2/3=77/4.
\]

The actual points are 1,1/2,-2,-1,8,11/2. On the positive ray the
derivative is r on [0,1/2], 1/2 on [1/2,1], r-1/2 on [1,3], and5/2
on [3,infinity). On the negative ray its magnitude is min(r,1).
Direct integration gives f(11/2)=77/8, consistent with the formula.
By contrast the exact K_5 value is max{1/35,4/23,1/3}=1/3.

## Interface still missing for the project target

The construction works for each chain satisfying (2)--(4), and these
conditions can be checked from the selected block sums and step values.
It does not establish the existence of a sufficiently strong feasible chain
for every schedule. The assertion that maximizing (5) over feasible chains
always gives (1-o(1))U_n^ZJ would be a new theorem-strength obligation.
No such assertion is assumed. The terms -O_i and E are genuine retained
history contributions; discarding them changes the construction and is not
a permitted constant-level approximation without a separate proof.

evidence: Use fact b98bb807d514e80d for the two legal bounds. Fix x,y>=0, set A=x+1>=1 and D=2y+1>=1, and vary the joining step b>=0. Define M(b)=max{1/[2(x+b+y)+1],(b-1)_+^2/[A^2 D]}. The first term strictly decreases in b; the second is zero up to1 and strictly increases afterward, so the unique minimizer occurs at their crossing b>1. Write t=b-1>0. This is an exact local minimax identity for every real nonnegative x,y, independent of chronology inside the two fixed-sum blocks. Fix any integer n>=0, L>0, and any predetermined finite nonnegative schedule h of length n for gradient descent x_{t+1}=x_t-(h_t/L)f'(x_t). Write W_n(h) for the supremum of 2(f(x_n)-f_star)/(L||x_0-x_star||^2) over all finite-dimensional convex differentiable functions with L-Lipschitz gradient, a minimizer x_star, and x_0!=x_star.

m_{i+1}=((b_i-1)m_i-O_i)/(1+s_{i+1}), O_{i+1}=O_i+s_i m_i.
Require m_i>0 for 0<=i<k and m_i>=m_{i-2} for 2<=i<k.
Define z_term=(b_{k-1}-1)m_{k-1}-O_{k-1}, and define m_old=0 if k=1 and m_old=m_{k-2} if k>=2. Require z_term>=(1+s_k)m_old.
Define e_term=sum_{0<=i<k, i congruent k mod 2}s_i m_i^2.

Then an explicitly constructed one-dimensional convex differentiable function f with L-Lipschitz derivative, f(0)=0=min f, and initial point x_0=1 realizes the full supplied GD schedule and has exactly
2 f(x_n)/L = 2e_term+2q z_term-(2s_k+1)q^2.
Consequently this expression is a lower bound for W_n(h). The largest value within the stated q interval is attained at
q_opt=max{m_old,z_term/(2s_k+1)}.

For h=(1,5,1,9,1), the checkpoint choice (5,9) has exact optimized payoff77/4, whereas K_5(h)=1/3.
No uniform comparison between F_ray_n and the Zhang–Jiang profile is asserted.

For any s_k>=0 the function q -> 2e_term+2q z_term-(2s_k+1)q^2 is a strictly concave quadratic. Its unconstrained maximum is z_term/(2s_k+1). evidence:
# P5: a concrete consistent branching policy
Status: complete support construction and two quantitative tests; unverified. No new verification allocation requested. The exact-profile comparison remains open.

## 1. Scalar interpolation state

Normalize L=1, choose minimizer0 and initial point1. A history H is a finite set of gradient knots (y,v), always including(0,0), satisfying
0 <= (v-w)/(y-z) <=1 whenever y>z, and v=w when y=z.
Define
ell_H(x)=max_{(y,v) in H} [v-(y-x)_+],
u_H(x)=min_{(y,v) in H} [v+(x-y)_+].
Every monotone1-Lipschitz derivative interpolating H lies between these envelopes. Conversely both envelopes are global monotone1-Lipschitz functions interpolating H: max/min preserve nondecreasingness and the upper bound1 on increments, and the pairwise history conditions force equality at each stored knot. In particular they agree at0 with value0. Thus ell_H<=u_H. Adding a knot(x,g) preserves the history conditions exactly when ell_H(x)<=g<=u_H(x).

For an endpoint x, the largest normalized objective among all convex1-smooth functions whose derivatives interpolate H and whose value at0 is0 is
Phi(H,x)=2 integral_0^x u_H(z) dz if x>=0,
Phi(H,x)=-2 integral_x^0 ell_H(z) dz if x<=0.
For the first case take derivative u_H globally, and for the second take derivative ell_H globally. These derivatives are continuous, monotone and1-Lipschitz, vanish at0, and integrate to globally convex1-smooth functions minimized at0. The envelopes bound every possible derivative pointwise, which proves maximality with the appropriate integration orientation. The chosen objective therefore reproduces every stored gradient. It is piecewise quadratic with finitely many pieces and lives in dimension1.

This is a derivative-oracle construction: no function values were supplied to GD and none need to be preserved except the final chosen value. The whole h is fixed first. An adversary's random choices construct a function afterward whose exact gradient trajectory is that path; they do not change the GD steps adaptively.

## 2. Actual policy, not optimization over all gradient choices

Fix h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}) with n>=1 and arbitrary finite nonnegative entries. For each j in{0,...,n-1}, put P_j=sum_{s<j}h_s and c=1/(1+P_j). Policy D_j first forces g_i=c for0<=i<=j. Its points are x_i=1-c sum_{s<i}h_s>=c for i<=j, so these knots are legal with(0,0). After step j,
x_{j+1}=c(1-h_j).
For every t=j+1,...,n-1 let S_t=sum_{s=t}^{n-1}h_s, let H_t be ALL prior knots together with(0,0), and compute
v_t = u_{H_t}(x_t) if x_t>=0, and ell_{H_t}(x_t) if x_t<0,
w_t = projection of x_t/(1+2S_t) onto [ell_{H_t}(x_t),u_{H_t}(x_t)].
With probability1/2 choose g_t=v_t; otherwise choose g_t=w_t. Coins at successive stages are independent. Add(x_t,g_t), then take the fixed GD step x_{t+1}=x_t-h_t g_t. Repeated points, zero steps and x_t=0 are harmless because their feasible intervals force the stored gradient.

After the final step select the global objective attaining Phi(H_n,x_n). This is a finite law on at most2^{n-j-1} legal functions, each with initial squared distance1. The expected normalized error D_j(h) has the exact recurrence
E_n(H,x)=Phi(H,x),
E_t(H,x)=(1/2)E_{t+1}(H union{(x,v)},x-h_t v)
        +(1/2)E_{t+1}(H union{(x,w)},x-h_t w),
with v,w defined by the displayed policy at state(H,x,t).
D_j(h) is E_{j+1} evaluated after its forced prefix. This recurrence is the payoff of two specified actions, not a supremum over all feasible gradients. It is an exact symbolic specification; no exponential enumeration has been run.

Each selected function is legal path by path. Thus W_n(h)>=D_j(h) for every j. Combined with the verified global/single-cut functional K_n from fact b98bb807d514e80d,
W_n(h)>=B_n^branch(h):=max{K_n(h), max_{0<=j<n}D_j(h)}.
One may choose the j with largest expectation after seeing h, or choose a point mass on a sufficiently good leaf. No infimum/expectation interchange is used. This notation B_n^branch is distinct from the benchmark denominator B_n.

## 3. Exact stopping event recovers the selected-cut value

Suppose h_j>1 and j<n-1. Write R=c(h_j-1)>0 and T=S_{j+1}. The first point on the negative half-line is -R, with no negative gradient knots yet. Therefore the feasible interval is[-R,0]. On its w-branch, the chosen gradient is -a, where a=R/(1+2T).
All later points remain <=-a, because total remaining displacement is aT and -R+aT=-a(1+T)<=-a.
The steep envelope at these points is -a. The later tail proposal is at most -a: if s is the tail sum already used, the ratio of its magnitude to a is
(1+2T-s)/(1+2T-2s)>=1.
Thus clamping selects -a. Both actions hence coincide thereafter, so this branch exactly follows an asymmetric Huber tail.
The terminal envelope on the negative half-line is max(z,-a); hence its normalized objective is
R^2/(1+2T)=(h_j-1)^2/[(1+P_j)^2(1+2T)].
The event has probability1/2, giving D_j(h) at least half of that cut term. At j=n-1 there is no coin; the maximal endpoint value is R^2, exactly the cut term with T=0.

This confirms normalization and chronology, but the half-cut bound alone is only a check: K_n already retains the full cut maximum. The benefit sought from D_j is in branches that continue through multiple sign changes and record excursions.

## 4. Quantitative multi-excursion test on the linear schedules

Take n>=4 and h_t=t+1. Choose j=2, so P_j=1+2=3 and c=1/4. The forced prefix has
x_0=1, x_1=3/4, x_2=1/4, x_3=-1/2.
On the event that every later coin takes the steep action, the trajectory is exactly GD on the function with derivative
q(z)=z for z<=1/4,
q(z)=1/4 for1/4<=z<=1,
q(z)=z-3/4 forz>=1.
This is a single global monotone1-Lipschitz derivative. Its derivative values equal the selected extremal envelope at every new query; adding such a knot does not change the pertinent extremal envelope. Positive knots cannot tighten the negative lower envelope beyond z, and negative knots on q(z)=z cannot tighten the positive upper envelope below min(z,1/4+(z-1)_+). Thus induction proves this entire event, not only its initial portion.
In particular x_4=3/2. Thereafter signs alternate and |x_t|>=3/2. For negative x_t the next magnitude is t|x_t|. For positive x_t, t>=4,
x_{t+1}=-t x_t+(3/4)(t+1)<0,
and
|x_{t+1}|>=((t-1)/2)|x_t|>=(t/4)|x_t|,
using |x_t|>=3/2. The last inequality and t>=4 preserve the lower bound3/2.
Therefore
|x_n| >= (3/2) product_{t=4}^{n-1}(t/4).
The chosen final envelope has objective at least that of the displayed global q. Integrating q shows 2f(z)=z^2 for negative z; for positive z>=3/2 it is (z-3/4)^2+3/8>=z^2/4. Hence every terminal point on this event satisfies
2f(x_n) >= (9/16) [product_{t=4}^{n-1}(t/4)]^2.
There are n-3 fair coins after the forced prefix, so
D_2(h) >= 2^{-(n-3)}(9/16)[product_{t=4}^{n-1}(t/4)]^2. (L)
The right side diverges faster than any fixed power of n. For example, from t>=8 each factor in the product is at least2, and the factorial expression gives the full growth:
product_{t=4}^{n-1}(t/4)=(n-1)!/[6*4^{n-4}].
This analytic event calculation uses no numerical sweep or path enumeration.
By contrast, accepted fact b98bb807d514e80d proves K_n(h)<=16/n^2 for the same linear schedules. Thus this actual branching policy detects objective mass missed by every single-cut term on that family. It is a mechanism advance, not an all-schedule lower bound.

## 5. Guarded-long-step test

For h=(1,H,1), H>1, choose j=1. Then c=1/2 and the forced points are1,1/2,-(H-1)/2. On the final interior branch, probability1/2, the gradient is x_2/3 and the envelope is a left Huber tail. Its normalized error is (H-1)^2/12. Consequently
D_1(1,H,1)>=(H-1)^2/24.
This avoids the fixed-one-curvature annihilation that affected the previous two-curvature subclass. It does not imply any bound for arbitrary schedules by itself.

## 6. Remaining obligation and next adversarial tests

No proof presently compares B_n^branch(h) uniformly to U_n^ZJ. The statement
for every epsilon>0 there exists N_epsilon independent of h such that
B_n^branch(h)>=(1-epsilon)U_n^ZJ for all n>=N_epsilon and h>=0
would by itself solve the affirmative direction; it cannot be called a support lemma.
The concrete next test is whether the fair-coin continuation loses nonvanishing mass on recursive schedules near the ZJ sum threshold, even when B_n^branch includes the exact K_n fallback. If it does, change the continuation probabilities or replace the scalar geometry, not merely append another restricted-family no-go. The successful linear/guarded tests do not establish that the comparison is true.
