## 1. Results and exact scope

Fix an integer m>=1536 and, throughout every child, use

    lambda=1+sqrt(2), epsilon=1/(4m), beta=1-epsilon,
    c=lambda*(1+epsilon), a=beta/c, d_j=a*c^j,
    H_0=(), H_(j+1)=(H_j,1+d_j,H_j), 0<=j<m,
    S_j=sum H_j, A_j=1+S_j, D_m=1+2*S_m,
    n_m=2^m-1, ell=1+a, b=a*beta.

These are local hierarchy symbols. In particular b is a plateau factor,
not either clipping level. d_m is an auxiliary radius, not another step.
The largest actual level is m-1. All original physical steps, including
the final level-zero leaf ell, are retained.

For b_plus,b_minus>0 and kappa_plus,kappa_minus in[0,1], define ONE static
function on the whole line by

    g(x)=min(kappa_plus*x,b_plus), x>=0,
    g(x)=max(kappa_minus*x,-b_minus), x<=0,
    f(x)=integral_0^x g(t) dt.

Let Psi_j(s) be its actual full-word GD output from s using H_j,
for0<=j<=m, including the identity Psi_0.
The principal new candidate is the ENTIRE common-curvature law:

    kappa_plus=kappa_minus=kappa in(0,1] implies
    sup_(s!=0) 2*f(Psi_m(s))/s^2
          = kappa/(1+2*kappa*S_m).                    (1.1)

This is for EVERY fixed positive pair b_plus,b_minus, all starts, and
arbitrary dependence of parameters on m. It includes every effective-step
regime kappa*h<1, =1, between1 and2, =2 and >2. The supremum is attained on
each saturated ray. Taking the supremum also over common kappa gives1/D_m.

For independent positive curvatures put K=max(kappa_plus,kappa_minus), and

    kappa_0=1/(1+d_(m-2)).

A second exact candidate covers the complete low-curvature region:

    0<K<=kappa_0 implies
    sup_(s!=0) 2*f(Psi_m(s))/s^2
          = K/(1+2*K*S_m).                            (1.2)

Every trajectory here has at most one sign change, since only the root
can cross zero. Section12 proves this using the two different curvatures,
not by replacing the function with a common-curvature function.

When exactly one curvature is zero and the other is kappa>0, the exact
positive-own-distance profile is kappa/(1+2*kappa*S_m), for every
nonnegative physical word, not just H_m. If both vanish the objective is
zero; no quotient by a zero closest distance is taken.

The remaining independent-positive-curvature region is

    K>kappa_0, kappa_plus!=kappa_minus, both positive, (1.3)

with all clipping levels and starts retained. No full profile is asserted
there. Section13 gives a legal genuinely clipped full-word counterexample
to transplanting the common-curvature radial lemma using K. Its exact
objective is below1/D_m, so it refutes that intermediate reduction, not
the desired objective bound or the original minimax statement.

The original normalization remains W_n(h)=sup 2(F(x_n)-F_star)/
(L*||x_0-x_star||^2), with W=2R and the original all-n/all-nonnegative-h
quantifiers. A restricted scalar family upper bound is not an upper bound
on full W. Accepted fact931b9653ce0f7201 is used only for its unconditional
B_(n_m)/D_m<47/50; its full-W hypothesis17/(16D_m) stays unproved. Prior
unit-core draft987e49ed35eb24e7 was read as awareness; all premises needed
here are derived jointly. No assertion from the unclipped two-ray draft
bf10ce01c54882c8 is imported.

## 2. Static legality, all rows, and closest distance

For a ray with positive curvature kappa_sigma, let
u_sigma=b_sigma/kappa_sigma. With r=|x| on that ray,

    f(x)=kappa_sigma*r^2/2, 0<=r<=u_sigma,
    f(x)=b_sigma*r-b_sigma^2/(2*kappa_sigma), r>=u_sigma.

For zero curvature that entire ray has f=g=0. The derivative g is
continuous and nondecreasing. On every linear piece its slope is in[0,1].
Partitioning any interval at the finite breakpoints proves
|g(x)-g(y)|<=|x-y|. Thus f is finite, convex, differentiable and globally
1-smooth. For arbitrary advertised L>0, use F=L*f and physical steps h/L;
the scalar iterates are unchanged and the normalized objective is the
same.

The complete minimum set C is {0} when both curvatures are positive;
(-infinity,0] when only kappa_plus is positive; [0,infinity) when only
kappa_minus is positive; and the whole line when both are zero. The minimum
value is0. When the closest initial distance is positive it is exactly
|s| in the first three cases. Starts already in C are stationary and have
zero gap. In the identically zero case every original admissible pair has
zero payoff, while the closest-distance quotient is left undefined.

For every physical index, including the unqueried terminal, define

    x_0=s, x_(i+1)=x_i-h_i*g(x_i),
    g_i=g(x_i), f_i=f(x_i), 0<=i<=n_m.

Every ordered original interpolation row follows directly. For x<y put
Delta=g(y)-g(x), so0<=Delta<=y-x. For x<=t<=y, monotonicity and smoothness
give

    g(t)-g(x)>=max(0,Delta-(y-t)),
    g(y)-g(t)>=max(0,Delta-(t-x)).

Integrating each inequality gives at least Delta^2/2. These are precisely
the two ordered inequalities

    Q_ij=f_i-f_j+g_i*(x_j-x_i)+(g_i-g_j)^2/2<=0.       (2.1)

Equal locations give equality. This treats every remote pair, every
revisit, all threshold equalities, the terminal, and all minimizers.
The full Gram matrix of the actual scalar displacement and gradients is
positive semidefinite because each quadratic form is a square of a real
linear combination. No formal gradient coordinate or row is removed.

Spatial scaling multiplies both clipping levels and the initial position
by the same factor and leaves curvature unchanged. Removing a common
curvature from g instead changes EVERY effective step. Section3 does that
change explicitly; no word is silently replaced or reset.

## 3. Common curvature: effective word and constants

For common kappa>0 put u=b_plus/kappa and v=b_minus/kappa, reflect if
necessary so u>=v, and write f=kappa*F, where

    G(x)=F'(x)=clip(x,[-v,u]).

The actual update becomes x -> x-alpha_i*G(x), with alpha_i=kappa*h_i
at physical index i. Separately define the following level quantities:

    delta=1-kappa, R_j=kappa*d_j,
    t_j=kappa*(1+d_j)=kappa+R_j,
    e_j=t_j-1=R_j-delta,
    M_j=kappa*S_j, C_j=1+M_j=kappa*A_j+delta.

Here t_j is a level-j effective bridge, not physical time. The effective
word is exactly kappa*H_m. Its masses obey

    C_(j+1)=2*C_j+e_j, M_(j+1)=2*M_j+t_j,
    R_(j+1)=c*R_j.                                  (3.1)

Using epsilon<=1/6144 and sqrt(2)<17/12 gives

    12/5<c<49/20, beta>99/100,
    2/5<a<1/2, 2/5<b<1/2, c*b=beta^2<1.             (3.2)

For the lower bound on b, a>99/245 and therefore
b>9801/24500>2/5. The upper bounds use c>lambda and beta<1.
Let eta=a/(c-2). Since c(c-2)>lambda(lambda-2)=1,
0<eta<1. Summing the literal word gives

    A_j=(1-eta)*2^j+eta*c^j,
    A_j>=d_j/(c-2), A_j<c^j for j>=1,
    d_j/A_j<c-2<1/2.                                (3.3)

The first identity follows from A_0=1 and A_(j+1)=2*A_j+d_j,
using2*eta+a=c*eta. Consequently

    M_j>=R_j/(c-2)-kappa,
    e_j/C_j<=d_j/A_j<1/2 whenever e_j>=0.            (3.4)

Also, with the local constant

    Q=1/(c-2)+1/c,

one has Q>1160/441>5/2>c. No evaluated hierarchy or numerical estimate
is used in these inequalities.

Every level-k occurrence in H_m has a literal H_k immediately before and
after it, so its physical prefix and suffix masses are at least S_k.
After its following H_k, the remaining suffix consists of increasing
ancestor levels, each followed by its full right child:

    H_k, t_(l_1),H_(l_1), ..., t_(l_r),H_(l_r),
    k<l_1<...<l_r<=m-1.                              (3.5)

The H symbols in this display have their effective steps kappa*H. This
is a decomposition of the actual binary tree: ascend past right-child
ancestors until reaching the next left-child ancestor, then take its
bridge and right child. At k=0 the first H_0 is empty. At the final leaf
there is no remaining component.

## 4. Exact signed step images and a monotone-block bound

For common curvature, an interval[-p,q] contains0 and its image under
a step t remains an interval containing0. If0<=t<=1, the map is
nondecreasing, and the exact endpoint magnitudes are

    p'=p-t*min(p,v), q'=q-t*min(q,u).                 (4.1)

If t>=1, writing e=t-1, the exact endpoint magnitudes are

    p'=max(e*min(q,u),p-t*v),
    q'=max(e*min(p,v),q-t*u).                        (4.2)

For(4.2), each ray has slope-e in its core and slope1 on its tail;
its extrema are at a threshold or an endpoint. The first terms in the
maxima are nonnegative. Formulae(4.1)-(4.2) coincide at t=1 and include
all endpoint/threshold equalities. At t=2 the core slope is-1, and for
t>2 it is less than-1; neither case is omitted.

Write Phi_j(p,q) for the TWO nonnegative endpoint magnitudes of the
exact image Psi_j([-p,q]). Continuity makes both endpoints attained.
Interval inclusion makes Phi_j coordinatewise nondecreasing. Composition
with(4.1) or(4.2) is exact for the whole interval. Bounds below therefore
apply to compatible actual child histories, not independently chosen
child maximizers. This interface is used only symbolically.

Consider any block all of whose effective steps lie in[0,1], of total
mass M. Sign is preserved, and on a ray with threshold w its radius map
is a composition of r -> r-t*min(r,w). Each such map is convex and
nondecreasing on r>=0, fixes0, and has slopes1-t,1. The complete map is
therefore convex, nondecreasing and fixes0. In particular

    B(theta*r)<=theta*B(r), 0<=theta<=1.             (4.3)

There is also an explicit upper bound by the clipped continuous flow:

    B(r)<=V_M(r;w),
    V_M(r;w)=r*exp(-M),                       r<=w,
             r-M*w,                         r>=w and M<=r/w-1,
             w*exp(r/w-1-M),                 r>=w and M>=r/w-1. (4.4)

Here(4.4) is an inequality proved from the displayed elementary maps,
not an invocation of an external flow theorem. One step stays linear
on a tail until the threshold. A crossing step has residual radius
w*(1-z)<=w*exp(-z), z>=0. A core step satisfies1-t<=exp(-t).
The displayed maps V form a semigroup by direct substitution and are
nondecreasing in their input. Induction over the block proves(4.4).
Increasing the ray threshold can only decrease the radius map for these
nondecreasing steps, so a smaller comparison threshold is legitimate.

If the terminal radius exceeds w, all queried radii are at least that
terminal radius, and every gradient radius is at least w. Hence

    B(r)<=max(w,r-M*w).                              (4.5)

This last assertion also follows directly from the physical updates.

## 5. All common curvatures: the starting level for plateaus

The plateau factor is the SAME b from(3.2). Define a starting level J.
If kappa*ell>=1, set J=1. If kappa*ell<1, let J be the smallest positive
integer with R_J>=delta, if such an integer is needed within the word.
Then

    delta<=R_J<c*delta,
    every physical step in H_J is less than1.       (5.1)

If no such J occurs before m, the entire word is sign preserving and is
already covered by Section9. Whenever this section is used, J<=m.
For all j>=J the bridges have e_j>=0 and e_j<=R_j.

The base plateau is, for every integer r>=0,

    Phi_J(R_J*w*b^r,R_J*w*b^r)
              <=(w*b^(r+1),w*b^(r+1)).             (5.2)

Here choose w=u for1<=u/v<=2, and w=v for u/v>=2.
We prove both choices directly.

First take kappa*ell<1. Put R=R_J and M=M_J. By(3.4),(5.1),

    M>=R/(c-2)-kappa, delta>R/c,
    M>=R/(c-2)-1+delta.                              (5.3)

For w=v, both ray thresholds are at least v, so(4.4) applies with
comparison threshold v. If R<=1, the output divided by v is at most

    R*exp(-M)<=exp(1)*R*exp(-Q*R)<=1/Q<2/5<b.

The middle function has derivative exp(1-Q*R)*(1-Q*R), so its global
maximum is1/Q at R=1/Q. If R>=1, (5.3) gives M>R-1, and the output
is at most exp(R-1-M)<exp(-(Q-1)*R)<2/5. The last bound follows from
Q>5/2, R>=1, and exp(z)>=1+z. This proves(5.2) at r=0.

For w=u and u/v<=2, both thresholds are at least u/2. Compare with
threshold u/2. If R<=1/2 the same R*exp(-M) bound is below b. If
R>=1/2, (5.3) gives M>2*R-1, and the output divided by u is at most

    (1/2)*exp(2*R-1-M)
       <(1/2)*exp(-(Q-2)*R)
       <=(1/2)/(1+1/4)=2/5<b.

Here Q-2>1/2 and R>=1/2. Convexity(4.3), separately on each ray,
now proves(5.2) for all r>=0 in BOTH cases.

If kappa*ell>=1, put e_0=kappa*ell-1 in[0,a]. Also R_1=kappa*beta<1.
For w=v the entire base interval is in the common core, so both endpoint
magnitudes are e_0*R_1*v*b^r<=a*beta*v*b^r=b*v*b^r.
For w=u and u/v<=2, apply(4.2). The core extremum is at most
e_0*R_1*u*b^r<=b*u*b^r. The only additional tail term is

    R_1*u*b^r-t_0*v
       <=b^r*(R_1*u-t_0*v)
       <=b^r*u*kappa*(beta-ell/2)<=b^(r+1)*u.

Indeed beta-ell/2<=b, since
b-beta+ell/2=(1+a)/2-beta*(1-a)>(3*a-1)/2>0;
if beta-ell/2 is negative the desired upper bound remains immediate.
This proves the base plateau in every case, including kappa*ell=1.

For the large-ratio proof we also need the positive endpoint at the
larger base radius:

    second coordinate of Phi_J(c*R_J*v,c*R_J*v)<=v. (5.4)

In the low-curvature base, negative inputs stay negative. A positive
input has threshold at least2v. If c*R<=2, (4.4) bounds the positive
endpoint divided by v by
exp(1)*c*R*exp(-Q*R)<=c/Q<1. If c*R>=2, it is bounded by

    2*exp(c*R/2-1-M)
       <2*exp(-(Q-c/2)*R)
       <=2*exp(-(2*Q/c-1))<2/exp(1)<1.

The same inequalities show that the threshold is reached before the
end; Q>c is sufficient. In the high-curvature base, a negative input
can return to at most e_0*v<=a*v. A positive core input has nonpositive
output. A positive saturated input at most c*R_1*v has output at most
kappa*(c*beta-2*ell)*v<0, because c<49/20 and2*ell>14/5.
Thus(5.4) holds in this case too.

## 6. Ratio at most two: exact capture and all higher plateaus

Assume1<=u/v<=2. For every j<=m,

    Psi_j([-C_j*v,C_j*u])=[-v,u].                   (6.1)

An exterior start x>=C_j*u stays positive saturated at every query
and ends at x-M_j*u; the negative exterior has the analogous affine
formula. Indeed each physical prefix has mass at most M_j, leaving
radius at least its threshold. This proves the exterior assertion
without any sign assumption on core slopes.

For(6.1), the empty child is the identity. If(6.1) holds for j, the
first child of the parent interval has exact endpoint magnitudes
(C_j+t_j)*v and(C_j+t_j)*u, by the just proved exterior formula and
its central capture interval. If t_j<=1, (4.1) sends these to C_j*v
and C_j*u. If t_j>=1, (4.2) does the same: its cross terms satisfy
e_j*u<=C_j*v and e_j*v<=C_j*u by e_j/C_j<1/2 and u/v<=2. The
second child then gives exactly[-v,u]. This completes the induction.

We extend(5.2) to every j>=J, with w=u. Suppose it holds for j.
For the unscaled parent radius c*R_j*u, (6.1) and its exterior
branches bound the first-child endpoints by

    p<=max(v,c*R_j*u-M_j*v),
    q<=max(u,c*R_j*u-M_j*u).

The bridge has e_j>=0. Its core cross terms are at most R_j*u.
Its negative tail term is at most
max(-e_j*v,c*R_j*u-(M_j+t_j)*v), and its positive tail term is at
most max(-e_j*u,(c*R_j-M_j-t_j)*u). Both are at most R_j*u because

    M_j+t_j=kappa*A_j+R_j
              >=(1+1/(c-2))*R_j,
    (c-1)*R_j*(u/v)<=2*(c-1)*R_j<=M_j+t_j.

The last inequality uses c-2<1/2. Thus the ACTUAL bridge image is
contained in[-R_j*u,R_j*u], and the second child's plateau bounds
both terminal endpoints by b*u.

For r>=1, the parent radius is
c*R_j*u*b^r=(c*b)*R_j*u*b^(r-1)<=R_j*u*b^(r-1).
The first-child plateau bounds its image by u*b^r on both sides.
Since2*b<1, this interval is inside both core thresholds. The bridge
multiplies absolute values by e_j<=R_j. The second child's plateau
at r then gives u*b^(r+1) on both sides. This proves

    Phi_j(R_j*u*b^r,R_j*u*b^r)
                  <=(u*b^(r+1),u*b^(r+1))          (6.2)

for every j>=J and every integer r>=0.

## 7. Ratio at least two: joint drift, returns and plateaus

Assume u>=2v. For every j>=J, prove together

    |Psi_j(s)|<=max(v,|s|-M_j*v/3) for every real s, (7.1)
    Phi_j(R_j*v*b^r,R_j*v*b^r)
                  <=(v*b^(r+1),v*b^(r+1)), r>=0.   (7.2)

The base plateau was proved in Section5. If the base block has steps
less than1, compare both rays with the smaller threshold v, as justified
after(4.4), and apply(4.5). This proves(7.1). For the high-curvature leaf base,
a negative-to-positive output is at most e_0*v<v. A positive output
larger than v must come from a positive saturated input and loses t_0*u.
A negative output-p with p>v, from a negative input, loses t_0*v.
From a positive input s it satisfies p<=e_0*s. If e_0=0 this is
impossible; otherwise e_0<=a<1/2 gives
s-p>[(1-e_0)/e_0]*v>v>t_0*v/3, since t_0<3/2.
These cases prove the base drift.

We first describe a consequence of already proved lower-level plateaus.
Any negative-to-positive crossing at level k>=J lands at most e_k*v
<=R_k*v. Its following actual H_k captures it to b*v. Each later
ancestor in(3.5) sees radius at most b*v<v, has core multiplier
of magnitude e_l<=R_l, and its H_l captures it again to b*v.
If the high-curvature case permits a level-zero crossing, its landing
is at most e_0*v<=a*v<v. If it is the final leaf that is the actual
terminal. Otherwise its next ancestor has level at least1 and the
same plateau argument applies. In the low-curvature case levels k<J
cannot cross at all. Thus whenever the needed proper-child plateaus
are available, a negative-to-positive return implies terminal radius
at most a*v. A zero hit stays zero. This consequence is used only with
levels strictly below the block whose drift or plateau is being proved.

In particular, for a child H_j with j>J, the positive endpoint at input
radius c*R_j*v is at most a*v. A trajectory with a return has that bound.
Without such a return, any positive terminal must come from an entirely
positive trajectory. Its root level j-1 has t_(j-1)>=1. Remaining positive
there forces a saturated root query, and all earlier positive queries
are saturated because positions decrease. Its initial s must satisfy

    s>=(M_(j-1)+t_(j-1))*u
       >=2*(1+1/(c-2))*R_(j-1)*v
       >c^2*R_(j-1)*v=c*R_j*v.                     (7.3)

The strict comparison follows from c^2<25/4 and
2*(1+1/(c-2))>58/9>25/4. This contradicts the input radius.
For j=J the necessary bound by v is(5.4). Therefore in EVERY induction
step the first child's positive endpoint is at most v.

Suppose both(7.1)-(7.2) hold at j. Write R=R_j, M=M_j, t=t_j,
e=e_j. At parent input radius c*R*v, the first child has

    p<=max(v,(c*R-M/3)*v), q<=v.

Also p<=(kappa+2*R)*v. Indeed kappa+2*R>=1 because R>=delta, and

    (c-2)*R<=kappa+M/3

follows from M>=R/(c-2)-kappa and(c-2)^2<1/3. Formula(4.2) now
puts BOTH bridge endpoint magnitudes at most R*v: e*q<=R*v,
p-t*v<=R*v, e*min(p,v)<=R*v, and q-t*u<=0. The second child's
plateau proves the parent plateau at r=0. For r>=1 the geometric
argument of Section6 applies with w=v: c*b<1 places the first child
in its previous radius, its image is in the common core, and e<=R
allows the second plateau. Thus(7.2) is proved at j+1 BEFORE its drift.

For the parent drift write y=Psi_j(s), z=y-t*G(y), w=Psi_j(z).
Only |w|>v needs proof. If w>v, the return consequence, using the
already available proper-child plateaus, excludes any negative-to-
positive crossing. The whole trajectory is then positive. Its gradient
at every query is at least min(w,u)>v, so
s-w>=M_(j+1)*v, stronger than required.

Let w=-p with p>v. Child drift and child plateau give respectively

    |z|>=p+M*v/3, |z|>R*v.                          (7.4)

There are three possible bridge cases.

A. If z>0, a negative y could land at most e*v<=R*v, contradicting
(7.4). Thus y>0 stays positive across the bridge. Because t>=1,
this query is saturated and y=z+t*u>u. The first child's terminal y>u
excludes a return; all of its queries are positive saturated. Hence
s=z+(M+t)*u>=p+M*v/3+(M+t)*v>=p+(2*M+t)*v/3.

B. If z<0 and y<0, a core input would be nonnegative after the bridge.
Thus the query is negative saturated, |y|=|z|+t*v>v, and applying child
drift to the first child yields
|s|>=|y|+M*v/3>=p+2*M*v/3+t*v>=p+(2*M+t)*v/3.
The inequality |y|>v also follows from R+t=kappa+2*R>=1.

C. If z<0 and y>0, then |z|<=e*min(y,u). By(7.4), e<=R implies
y>v and min(y,u)>v. The first-child output y>v excludes returns, so
that entire child is positive and

    s>=y+M*min(y,u).

If y<=u, then |z|=e*y and
s-|z|>=(1+M-e)*y. If y>=u, then |z|=t*u-y and
s-|z|>=2*y+(M-t)*u>=(1+M-e)*u. In either case

    3*(1+M-e)-(M+t)
       =6-4*kappa+2*M-4*R
       >=6*delta+2*R*(1/(c-2)-2)>=0.                (7.5)

In particular1+M-e>0, and s-|z|>=(M+t)*v/3.
Combining with(7.4) gives s>=p+(2*M+t)*v/3.

Zero bridge inputs or outputs cannot occur in these cases. The cases
are exhaustive. Since M_(j+1)=2*M+t, they prove(7.1) at j+1 and
complete the joint induction. All child histories and both endpoints
remain actual. No unit-core positive-tail assertion was used.

For the FULL H_m, the same physical suffix argument now gives

    a negative-to-positive crossing => |Psi_m(s)|<=a*v. (7.6)

The final leaf uses a*v, not b*v; it has not been deleted.

## 8. Radial consequence and exact overlap of curvature ranges

Either plateau(6.2) with w=u or(7.2) with w=v implies

    |Psi_j(s)|<=|s|/R_j for0<|s|<=R_j*w, j>=J.      (8.1)

Choose an integer r>=0 such that
R_j*w*b^(r+1)<|s|<=R_j*w*b^r. The plateau bounds the output by
w*b^(r+1)<|s|/R_j. If an amplitude is a geometric boundary, take it
as the upper boundary of its next cell. Zero maps to zero. This covers
every real amplitude in the specified interval, not a sampled mesh.

We need the final comparison

    R_m^2>=1+2*kappa*S_m.                            (8.2)

It holds for EVERY kappa>=kappa_0=1/(1+d_(m-2)). Here is an explicit

Neither result excludes other metrics, other terminal probabilities, other

    C_0=B_0=1,

## 4. Complete original-coordinate factor and signed array, jointly derived

Normalize L=1 and x_star=g_star=f_star=0. Keep the vectors
x_0,g_0,...,g_n arbitrary and independent, and substitute only the
actual update x_i=x_0-sum_(j<i)h_j g_j. For original samples use

    Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2.

Actual interpolable jets have Q_ij<=0. For i<n set y_i=x_i-g_i and
Delta_i=f_i-||g_i||^2/2; star quantities vanish. Let T be lower triangular
with T_ii=1, T_ij=h_j for j<i, and zero otherwise. Then

    y=e*x_0-Tg, g=T^(-1)(e*x_0-y), t=Te.             (4.1)

This is an invertible change on the entire original space. Explicitly,
with pi_i=product_(j<i)(1-h_j),

          +sum_(j<i)h_j product_(j<r<i)(1-h_r)y_j.

The update x_(i+1)=(1-h_i)x_i+h_i y_i now gives

    x_n=-s*x_0+k^T y, e^T k=1+s, T^T k=h.

For the last identity telescope each suffix:
k_i+h_i sum_(j>i)k_j=h_i. Thus e^T v=p+s. Set

    Cprob_i=p+sum_(j<=i)alpha_j,
    R_i=h_i Cprob_i-alpha_i=(T^T v)_i>0.

Strict positivity follows from
R_i=h_i(p+sum_(j<i)alpha_j)+(h_i-1)alpha_i. Also

    R_0=bp+a alpha_0<2p,
    H=p+s-v_0=p+alpha_0-s/a, 0<H<2p.                (4.2)

These use(3.4); the lower bound H>p-u_0 is positive. The actual terminal
center is V=-s*x_0+v^T y. In particular the free original terminal
gradient has not been identified with a queried gradient.

For any positive detail weights w_i, Ww=sum_i w_i, define

    K=diag(w)-w w^T/Ww, tbar_w=sum_i w_i t_i/Ww.

Let d be any real column with e^T d=0, and A any skew matrix with Ae=d.
The general form is A=(d w^T-w d^T)/Ww+B with B skew and Be=0.

    P=K+gamma v v^T, N=T^T(P+A).

Every finite scalar entry is explicitly

    N_ij=K_ij+A_ij+h_i sum_(r>i)(K_rj+A_rj)+gamma R_i v_j. (4.3)

The FULL signed array on the original indices is

    lambda_(n,star)=2p, lambda_(n,i)=2alpha_i,
    lambda_(j,n)=0 for j in {star,0,...,z},
    lambda_(i,j)=-N_ij for distinct i,j<n,
    lambda_(i,star)=mu_i=(Ne)_i=2p R_i+(T^T d)_i,

Write M0=e^T nu and M1=t^T nu. From(4.4), Ke=0, e^T v=p+s,

    M1=t^T Kt+gamma Uclock^2-2t^T alpha.              (5.1)

The first row of T^T is b e^T-a e_0^T. Hence

## 4. Complete original-coordinate factor and signed array, jointly derived

Normalize L=1 and x_star=g_star=f_star=0. Keep the vectors
x_0,g_0,...,g_n arbitrary and independent, and substitute only the
actual update x_i=x_0-sum_(j<i)h_j g_j. For original samples use

    Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2.

Actual interpolable jets have Q_ij<=0. For i<n set y_i=x_i-g_i and
Delta_i=f_i-||g_i||^2/2; star quantities vanish. Let T be lower triangular
with T_ii=1, T_ij=h_j for j<i, and zero otherwise. Then

    y=e*x_0-Tg, g=T^(-1)(e*x_0-y), t=Te.             (4.1)

This is an invertible change on the entire original space. Explicitly,
with pi_i=product_(j<i)(1-h_j),

    g_i=pi_i*x_0-y_i
          +sum_(j<i)h_j product_(j<r<i)(1-h_r)y_j.

The update x_(i+1)=(1-h_i)x_i+h_i y_i now gives

    x_n=-s*x_0+k^T y, e^T k=1+s, T^T k=h.

For the last identity telescope each suffix:
k_i+h_i sum_(j>i)k_j=h_i. Thus e^T v=p+s. Set

    Cprob_i=p+sum_(j<=i)alpha_j,
    R_i=h_i Cprob_i-alpha_i=(T^T v)_i>0.

Strict positivity follows from
R_i=h_i(p+sum_(j<i)alpha_j)+(h_i-1)alpha_i. Also

    R_0=bp+a alpha_0<2p,
    H=p+s-v_0=p+alpha_0-s/a, 0<H<2p.                (4.2)

These use(3.4); the lower bound H>p-u_0 is positive. The actual terminal
center is V=-s*x_0+v^T y. In particular the free original terminal
gradient has not been identified with a queried gradient.

For any positive detail weights w_i, Ww=sum_i w_i, define

    K=diag(w)-w w^T/Ww, tbar_w=sum_i w_i t_i/Ww.

Let d be any real column with e^T d=0, and A any skew matrix with Ae=d.
The general form is A=(d w^T-w d^T)/Ww+B with B skew and Be=0.
Define

    P=K+gamma v v^T, N=T^T(P+A).

Every finite scalar entry is explicitly

    N_ij=K_ij+A_ij+h_i sum_(r>i)(K_rj+A_rj)+gamma R_i v_j. (4.3)

The FULL signed array on the original indices is

    lambda_(n,star)=2p, lambda_(n,i)=2alpha_i,
    lambda_(j,n)=0 for j in {star,0,...,z},
    lambda_(i,j)=-N_ij for distinct i,j<n,
    lambda_(i,star)=mu_i=(Ne)_i=2p R_i+(T^T d)_i,
    lambda_(star,i)=nu_i=(N^T e)_i-2alpha_i
            =(Kt)_i+gamma Uclock v_i-(At)_i-2alpha_i. (4.4)

Diagonal multipliers are zero. Terminal signs pass for our alpha, but
none of the other signs is presumed. The outgoing prefix sum at i is
N_ii and the incoming prefix sum is N_ii-2alpha_i. Adding the actual
terminal edge2alpha_i gives zero total divergence at i. Terminal
divergence is2; optimum divergence is-2. Hence sampled values cancel in

    M(q)=q||x_0||^2-2f_n+sum_(i!=j)lambda_ij Q_ij.

For prefix indices Q_ij=Delta_i-Delta_j+<g_i,y_j-y_i>. Their remaining
quadratic term is -g^T N y. Inserting(4.1), using e^T K=0,
e^T A=-d^T and e^T P=2p v^T, gives
-<x_0,2p v^T y-d^T y>+y^T P y. Together with -2f_n, the actual outgoing
terminal rows give ||g_n-V||^2-||V||^2-2sum alpha_i Delta_i. The value terms
cancel as stated. Completing the common square therefore gives

    M(q)=||g_n+s*x_0-v^T y||^2+y^T K y
       +eta||v^T y-(p+s)x_0||^2
       +(q-p^2)||x_0||^2+<x_0,d^T y>.                (4.5)

Let ybar_w=sum_i w_i y_i/Ww and J=(1/4)sum_i d_i^2/w_i. Since sum d=0,
the FULL factor is

    M(q)=||g_n+s*x_0-v^T y||^2
       +sum_i w_i||y_i-ybar_w+(d_i/(2w_i))*x_0||^2
       +eta||v^T y-(p+s)x_0||^2
       +(q-p^2-J)||x_0||^2.                         (4.6)

The initial charge J is paid ONCE globally. All detail directions, the
common square and its real derivative, and the actual terminal square
remain. Full PSD is equivalent to q>=p^2+J. For necessity set scalar
x_0=1, y_i=c0-d_i/(2w_i), where
c0=1+[sum_i v_i d_i/(2w_i)]/(p+s), and set g_n=p. The terminal, detail
and common squares in(4.6) vanish; reconstruct every queried g_i with(4.1). This gives
M(q)=q-p^2-J. It is a formal-space test, not an interpolable instance.

For the actual common-gradient direction g_i=G at all queried indices,
y_i=x_0-t_i G. The full prefix quadratic after deleting only its terminal
square is

    (q-p^2)||x_0||^2-(d^T t)<x_0,G>
                 +(t^T Kt+eta Uclock^2)||G||^2.      (4.7)

Thus the real initial/common derivative is retained, and skew transport
cannot remove it.

## 5. Global load moments, exact skew completion and first-row moments

Write M0=e^T nu and M1=t^T nu. From(4.4), Ke=0, e^T v=p+s,
e^T A=-d^T and t^T At=0 give EXACTLY

    M0=2p Uclock+d^T t-2(1-p),
    M1=t^T Kt+gamma Uclock^2-2t^T alpha.              (5.1)

Any nonnegative incoming load must obey

    M0>=0, M1>=0, M0<=M1<=Tlast*M0.                  (5.2)

These are necessary screens for the full array, not sufficient signs.
They are invariant under every balanced skew re-selection keeping d.
For the isolated load problem they are also sufficient: the endpoint
column

    nu_target=((Tlast*M0-M1)/DeltaClock)e_0
                   +((M1-M0)/DeltaClock)e_z          (5.3)

is nonnegative and has precisely those two moments. This does not assert
that the induced finite interpolation multipliers have the needed signs.

Here is a literal skew completion for ANY specified nonnegative load with
the compatible moments. Put F=Kt+gamma Uclock v, r=F-2alpha-nu_target,
tmean_e=(e^T t)/n, cvec=t-tmean_e e, V_e=cvec^T cvec>0, and

    A0=(d e^T-e d^T)/n,
    fvec=r-tmean_e d+(d^T t)e/n,
    A=A0+(fvec cvec^T-cvec fvec^T)/V_e.              (5.4)

Compatibility gives e^T r=-d^T t and t^T r=0. Consequently
e^T fvec=0 and cvec^T fvec=0. Direct multiplication now proves Ae=d
and At=r, with both displayed terms skew. Thus(4.4) yields precisely
nu_target. Every entry is a displayed formula in the original indices;
there is no unknown feasible matrix or LP. Any other skew with the same
actions on e,t differs by C with Ce=Ct=0. Such C preserves the factor
and the incoming AND outgoing optimum loads, but may change finite rows.

The first row has two further necessary invariants. Define

    S0=sum_(j>0)N_0j,
    P0=sum_(j>0)(t_j-1)N_0j,
    G0=P0-DeltaClock*S0=sum_(j>0)(t_j-Tlast)N_0j.

The first row of T^T is b e^T-a e_0^T. Hence
N_00=-a K_00-b d_0+gamma R_0 v_0 and

    S0=a K_00+gamma R_0 H+d_0.                       (5.5)

To obtain the clock row, use
N_0j=-a K_0j+gamma R_0 v_j-b d_j-a A_0j.
Multiplication by(t_j-1) and substitution of At=F-2alpha-nu give

    P0=-2a(Kt)_0+gamma Uclock(R_0-a v_0)-2p R_0
                 -b(d^T t)+2a alpha_0+a nu_0+a d_0. (5.6)

In particular, C e=C t=0 cannot alter S0 or P0. If every finite first-row
multiplier is nonnegative, N_0j<=0, then the complete two-moment screen is

    S0<=0, DeltaClock*S0<=P0<=b*S0.                 (5.7)

Indeed b=t_1-1<=t_j-1<=DeltaClock. Its lower inequality is G0>=0.
When S0=0 it forces all off-diagonal entries to vanish, not just their sum.

## 6. Mechanism I: whole absolute-tail law, every balanced skew excluded

For arbitrary kappa>0 and tau>=0 fix

    w_i=kappa u_i, alpha_i=(1-p)rho_i,
    d=tau(rho-e_0),
    A=tau(rho e_0^T-e_0 rho^T)+B,
    B^T=-B, Be=0.                                  (6.1)

Here B is universally quantified for an obstruction, not offered as an
unknown sign-feasible construction. Every skew with Ae=d is included.
The exact single charge and clock variance are

    J=tau^2(1-rho_0)/(4kappa u_0),
    Vtail=sum_i u_i(t_i-tbar)^2,
    t^T Kt=kappa Vtail, d^T t=tau(tbar-1).           (6.2)

The charge follows by separately summing i=0 and i>0 in(4.6).
Equation(3.5) and pS=1-p now reduce(5.1) to

    M0=tau(tbar-1)-2p(1-p)tbar,
    M1=kappa Vtail+gamma Uclock^2-2(1-p)tbar.        (6.3)

Nonnegative nu requires

    tau>=2p(1-p)tbar/(tbar-1)>p.                    (6.4)

The strict inequality uses tbar>1 and p<1/2. The upper clock constraint
M1<=Tlast*M0, together with pTlast=1-bp, is

    kappa Vtail<=tau Tlast(tbar-1)
                     +2bp(1-p)tbar-gamma Uclock^2
                 <tau/p^2+3.                      (6.5)

Here Tlast,tbar<1/p,2b<3, and the dropped last term is nonpositive.
The other moment requirements in(5.2) still apply, but are not needed
for this contradiction.

For any center tbar, retaining only the adjacent final two terms gives

    Vtail>= [u_z u_(z-1)/(u_z+u_(z-1))]
                             (t_z-t_(z-1))^2>1.    (6.6)

This two-term minimum follows by completing its scalar square. Indeed
u_z>4/3,u_(z-1)>5/8 and t_z-t_(z-1)=1+beta>15/8 give the lower bound
(20/47)*(225/64)=4500/3008>1.

Suppose full PSD holds at q<=qtar. Since
qtar/p=17/[16(2-p)]<1, equation(4.6) implies

    kappa>=tau^2(1-rho_0)/(4p u_0).

Combine this with(6.5), divide by the positive tau, and use tau>p:

    (1-rho_0)Vtail/(4u_0)
      <tau(1-rho_0)Vtail/(4p u_0)
      <1/p^2+3/tau<1/p^2+3/p<2/p^2.

Consequently u_0>(1-rho_0)Vtail p^2/8>9p^2/80, contradicting(3.4).
This covers all m>=1536, all kappa>0,tau>=0, and EVERY balanced B.

For completeness, the outgoing optimum signs in this entire family pass.
Let F_i^u=u_i+h_i sum_(j>i)u_j>0. Then

    mu_0=2pR_0+a tau(1-rho_0)>0,
    mu_i=2pR_i+tau F_i^u/U>0 for i>0.

All terminal signs also pass. The contradiction is precisely between
incoming-optimum nonnegativity and the full global PSD charge. It does
not rely on either literal transport rejected previously, a finite-row
deletion, or a primal construction. Allowing tau<0 cannot save the family:
M0 in(6.3) would already be strictly negative.

## 7. Exact two-moment imbalance price

Before selecting the changed metric, record the exact charge for arbitrary
positive weights. Prescribe d_0=-r0, sum_i d_i=0 and d^T t=theta. Put

    Wplus=sum_(i>0)w_i, tplus=sum_(i>0)w_i t_i/Wplus,
    Vplus=sum_(i>0)w_i(t_i-tplus)^2>0.

The inequality Vplus>0 holds here because there are at least two distinct
noninitial clocks with positive weights. The unique minimum-energy choice
on i>0 is

    d_i=w_i[r0/Wplus
                  +(theta-r0(tplus-1))(t_i-tplus)/Vplus]. (7.1)

It has sum r0 and clock sum theta+r0 on i>0. If any other feasible
column differs by e_i^res on i>0, that difference has zero sum and zero
clock moment. Its weighted inner product with(7.1) vanishes, so the
energy increases by sum_(i>0)(e_i^res)^2/w_i. The minimum global charge is

    Jmin=r0^2/(4K_00)
                +(theta-r0(tplus-1))^2/(4Vplus).     (7.2)

The first term includes BOTH source and compensating mass:
1/K_00=1/w_0+1/Wplus. Thus paying the source alone misses a second
potentially large clock cost.

If d_0 is also selected to minimize energy at fixed theta, weighted
Cauchy--Schwarz gives the exact law

    d=(theta/(t^T Kt))Kt,
    J=theta^2/(4t^T Kt).                            (7.3)

Indeed Kt has entries w_i(t_i-tbar_w), and their squared inverse-weight
sum is t^T Kt. This attains the global lower bound and, for its resulting
d_0, also attains(7.2). This is the choice used next.

## 8. Mechanism II: explicit source/end metric and zero incoming load

Keep exactly the probabilities of Section3. Abbreviate Cclock=Uclock
within this section only, and choose

    theta=2(1-p)-2p Cclock=2p(1-p)tbar,
    Xreq=2(1-p)tbar-gamma Cclock^2
                         =theta/p-gamma Cclock^2,
    omega=p^2,
    what_i=1_(i=0)+1_(i=z)+omega rho_i,
    tbase=sum_i what_i t_i/(2+omega),
    Vbase=sum_i what_i(t_i-tbase)^2,
    ellw=Xreq/Vbase, w_i=ellw*what_i,
    K=diag(w)-w w^T/sum w,
    d=(theta/Xreq)Kt,
    nu_target=0.                                   (8.1)

These are actual scalar coefficient formulas from the original word.
In the suggested four-component parametrization they are
kappa_tail=ellw*omega/U, kappa_mass=0,
kappa_start=kappa_end=ellw. No coefficient is a matrix-feasibility oracle.

Bounds(3.6) give 1<theta<2 and

    0<gamma p Cclock^2/theta<1/512,
    (511/512)theta/p<Xreq<2/p.                      (8.2)

For theta>1 use p<1/128 and
pCclock<(p Cclock^2)/32<1/32768. Both endpoint weights of what are
at least1 at distinct clocks, so Vbase>0. Hence ellw>0 and ALL original
detail weights are positive. The identities t^T Kt=Xreq, sum d=0,
d^T t=theta and(7.3) are exact. In(5.1) both load moments are zero.
The identically zero nu_target is therefore a nonnegative load with the
required moments. Use the literal skew(5.4), with r=Kt+gamma Cclock v-2alpha,
and choose its remaining skew correction to be zero. This specifies
every entry of A and, through(4.3)--(4.4), every original multiplier.

It is useful to admit ANY extra skew C with Ce=Ct=0 when auditing this
fixed law: the coming obstruction covers all of them. Such C changes
neither the selected load nor the charge, and is not a proposed repair.

### 8.1 Full PSD and all optimum signs pass

The full charge is J=theta^2/(4Xreq), with no source-tail inverse loss.
Equations(8.2) give

    p^2+J<p^2+(256/511)p
            <(33/64)p<(17/32)p<qtar.               (8.3)

For the middle bound use p<1/128 and
1/128+256/511<33/64, equivalent to32768<33215.
The last bound follows from qtar/p=17/[16(2-p)]>17/32.
Consequently(4.6) is full PSD at the assigned target, with strict slack.
This construction really changes the failed invariant cost in Mechanism I.

Every terminal outgoing multiplier is positive; incoming terminal ones
vanish as required. Every incoming-optimum multiplier is exactly zero.
Every outgoing-optimum multiplier is positive as well. To see this, the
sign of d_i is the sign of t_i-tbar_w. These signs change only once, from
negative to positive; d_0<0<d_z. Every proper prefix sum of d is negative:
before the crossing all terms are nonpositive, and after the crossing the
remaining suffix is positive. Thus every suffix sum after i is positive
for i<z. If d_i<0, the earlier prefix is nonpositive, so
sum_(j>i)d_j>=-d_i and

    (T^T d)_i=d_i+h_i sum_(j>i)d_j
                           >=(h_i-1)(-d_i)>0.

If d_i>=0 the same expression is positive, including i=z because d_z>0.
Therefore mu_i=2pR_i+(T^T d)_i>0 at every original query.
The remaining finite signs must still be checked; PSD and these optimum
signs do not establish a certificate.

### 8.2 The finite first-row sum passes

Put Delta=DeltaClock, Y=-(Kt)_0=w_0(tbar_w-1)>0. Then
d_0=-theta Y/Xreq. Since

    K_00/Y=[1+omega(1-rho_0)]
              /[Delta(1+omega rbar)],
    rbar=sum_i rho_i(t_i-1)/Delta in[0,1],

we have K_00/Y<=(1+omega)/Delta. Now
Delta>3/(4p), omega<1/16384<1/8 and a<1/2 give
a(1+omega)/Delta<3p/4, while theta/Xreq>p. Hence

    S0=aK_00-theta Y/Xreq+gamma R_0H
                         <-pY/4+8p^2.              (8.4)

For an explicit lower bound on Y, define xclock_i=(t_i-1)/Delta in[0,1] and

    gbase=Vbase/Delta^2,
    fbase=(1+omega rho_0)(1+omega rbar)/(2+omega).

Retaining the two unit endpoint masses gives gbase>=1/2; centering at1/2
gives gbase<=1/2+omega/4<3/4. Also fbase>=1/(2+omega)>1/3.
Since Y=(Xreq/Delta)(fbase/gbase) and Xreq/Delta>511/512>3/4,
we get Y>1/3>1/4. Thus S0<-p/16+8p^2<0 because p<1/128.
The first-row total load is affordable and has the correct sign.

### 8.3 The finite first-row clock fails, for every Ce=Ct=0 correction

Write K_00=Xreq/Delta^2+eK and Y=Xreq/Delta+eY. The same scaled-weight
expressions give the uniform estimates

    |eY|<=4Xreq*omega/Delta,
    |eK|<=2Xreq*omega/Delta^2.                       (8.5)

To check them directly, 1/2-omega/4<=fbase<=1/2+omega, while
1/2<=gbase<=1/2+omega/4. Also

    K_00/ellw=
      [1+omega+omega^2 rho_0(1-rho_0)]/(2+omega)
                            lies in[1/2,1/2+omega/2].

Subtract gbase and use ellw=Xreq/(Delta^2 gbase)<=2Xreq/Delta^2.
These even give tighter estimates than(8.5).

Use(5.5)--(5.6), d^Tt=theta, d_0=-theta Y/Xreq and nu_0=0.
The endpoint-clock defect G0=P0-Delta*S0 is exactly

    G0=Gendpoint+Epert,
    Gendpoint=a(Xreq-Tlast*theta)/Delta
       +gamma R_0[Cclock-Tlast(p+s)+Delta v_0]
       -a gamma Cclock v_0+2a alpha_0,
    Epert=a(2eY-Delta eK)
                         +theta(Delta-a)eY/Xreq.    (8.6)

For the first line expand(5.6) and then substitute the two definitions
of eY,eK. Since Xreq<2/p, Delta>1/(2p), theta<2, a<1/2 and Delta>a,
(8.5) gives

    Epert<=|Epert|<28 omega=28p^2.                  (8.7)

Specifically the first term is at most10a Xreq omega/Delta<20omega,
and the second at most4theta omega<8omega.

The exact relation Xreq=theta/p-gamma Cclock^2 and
Tlast=1/p-b gives

    Xreq-Tlast*theta=b theta-gamma Cclock^2.

Using a>1/3,gamma>1,Delta<1/p, and dropping the negative terms
-gamma R_0 Tlast(p+s) and -a gamma Cclock v_0 in(8.6), we obtain

    Gendpoint<3p-(p/3)Cclock^2+4p Cclock+5u_0.

Indeed a b theta/Delta<3p because Delta>1/(2p);
gamma R_0<4p; gamma R_0 Delta v_0<4u_0; and2a alpha_0<u_0.
Combine with(3.4),(8.7) and p<1/128 to conclude

    G0<p[-Cclock^2/3+4Cclock+3+29p]
       <p[-Cclock^2/3+4Cclock+4]<0.                 (8.8)

The last sign follows from Cclock>32: Cclock^2/3>(32/3)Cclock,
so the bracket is less than -(20/3)Cclock+4<0.

But every nonpositive first-row off-diagonal entry would give
G0=sum_(j>0)(t_j-Tlast)N_0j>=0. Equation(8.8) is a contradiction.
At least one original finite lambda_(0,j)=-N_0j is therefore negative.
Every correction Ce=Ct=0 preserves this exact defect and cannot repair it.
This covers the full stated law for every SAME enclosing m>=1536, even
though its full PSD, all optimum signs and first-row sum already pass.

## 9. Scope audit, retrieval and handoff

All physical leaves, queried gradients, actual terminal gradient and
initial/common charge are present in the same original-coordinate identity.
There is no quotient, averaged terminal, dropped prefix interpolation row,
local budget recycling, or inferred primal interpolation from a formal test.
All signs needed for a certificate have explicit formulas. The positive
terminal and optimum signs are proved where claimed. Finite signs fail;
the report does not call their signed polynomial a feasible upper bound.

Mechanism I fixes w proportional to u, alpha proportional to u, p=1/(1+S),
and d=tau(rho-e_0), but includes EVERY skew with that imbalance. Changing
the imbalance's clock distribution, the metric or the probabilities lies
outside its exclusion. Mechanism II changes the metric and globally
minimizes the imbalance charge for its clock moment, but fixes nu=0 and
the displayed endpoint-dominated metric. Changing the incoming load or
substantially redistributing interior metric weight lies outside that
exclusion. The free skew corrections preserving the specified data have
been fully included in both obstruction scopes.

The two-moment minimum-price formula(7.2) exposes the distinction between
repairing the initial charge and repairing the clock charge. Mechanism II
also shows that satisfying both global load moments, the full PSD factor,
all optimum signs and the first-row SUM still need not satisfy the
first-row CLOCK. Those necessities should precede another local transport
proposal. No third mechanism is attempted or implied here.

# Full initial-state centered-triangle profile: explicit finite formula and unresolved comparison

JOINT UNVERIFIED. Worker max2, invocation75 after ended baseline74.
Project gd-exact-profile-20260926. Guidance c0b98bc7d6b0f588.
One analytical invocation, at most two substantive mechanisms. No new fact
is asserted: the formal gate is closed. All new arguments below form ONE
joint draft and do not use unverified sibling conclusions as premises.
Original target OPEN.

## 0. Verdict and exact scope

The body is exactly the assigned centered equilateral triangle in its actual
Euclidean plane. Every nonzero initial point, every original step, and the
actual terminal are included in the finite formula in Sections 7--10.
No scalar-axis extremality, fixed support, or selected inverse branch is
assumed in that formula.

The draft derives:

* Unique minimum0, smoothness1, complete projection guards and every original
  ordered interpolation row, including terminal rows.
* All starts in the entire triangle remain in the quadratic core through
  every physical prefix. Their normalized terminal payoff is exactly
  beta^(2n)c^(-2m).
* Each of the three full fixed-vertex classes and each of the three full
  fixed-edge classes has exact supremum1/D_m, attained. These classes include
  arbitrary permitted transverse coordinates, not only their axes.
* The unrestricted triangle supremum is attained. An explicit finite
  expression for it uses affine products, linear sign tests, and roots of
  polynomials of degree at most two; there is no residual continuous
  optimization, existence-of-transcript test, or unsolved matrix inequality.
  Its value is algebraic of degree at most8 over the rationals for each m.
* A concrete legal original-word prefix refutes the simple inradius-based
  radial drainage inequality that would otherwise have closed the comparison.

The finite expression is NOT evaluated, and its comparison with1/D_m or
17/(16D_m) is NOT proved. In particular, this is not a claim that the triangle
has exact optimum1/D_m, nor that it gives a nonvanishing improvement. The
first mechanism yields the geometric screens and obstruction; the second
eliminates the continuous variables in the full profile. No arbitrary-N
simplex theorem is claimed. The assignment permits a second triangle method
when the decisive first-method comparison remains unresolved, and that is
how the second mechanism is used here.

The exponential face list is a literal finite algebraic expression, not a
proposal to run an exhaustive search. No part of that list was enumerated or
evaluated by a mathematical program. It does not resolve the original
all-dimension/all-word minimax problem.

## 1. Parameters and body

Fix one integer m>=1536 throughout. Define

  epsilon=1/(4m), beta=1-epsilon, lambda=1+sqrt(2),
  c=lambda(1+epsilon), a=beta/c,
  H_0=(), H_(j+1)=(H_j,1+a*c^j,H_j), 0<=j<m,
  n=2^m-1, S=sum H_m, D_m=1+2S.

All children use these SAME parameters. The word has exactly n physical
steps, numbered0,...,n-1. Put h_i=(H_m)_i. Its last step is1+a.
Let

  v_1=(1,0), v_2=(-1/2,sqrt(3)/2), v_3=(-1/2,-sqrt(3)/2),
  D=conv{v_1,v_2,v_3},
  F(x)=max_(g in D) [x dot g-||g||^2/2],
  x_(i+1)=x_i-h_i grad F(x_i),
  E_m(x_0)=2F(x_n)/||x_0||^2, x_0!=0,
  V_triangle(m)=sup_(x_0!=0) E_m(x_0).

All norms and inner products are the usual real Euclidean ones. The three
vertices have norm1, sum0, and pairwise inner product-1/2. Consequently

  D={x: v_i dot x>=-1/2 for i=1,2,3},
  {x: ||x||<=1/2} subset D subset {x: ||x||<=1},
  -D subset 2D.

For each edge opposite v_i put n_i=-v_i, t_i=J n_i, where
J(u_1,u_2)=(-u_2,u_1), and b=sqrt(3)/2. Its endpoints are the two
points (1/2)n_i +/- b t_i.

The dihedral group generated by permutations of the vertices preserves D,
F, the GD maps, and E_m. This symmetry is recorded but is NOT used to replace
an arbitrary initial point by a symmetry axis.

## 2. Legality, full minimum, metric, and all original rows

Completing the square shows that the maximizer in F is the unique Euclidean
projection g=P_D(x). The defining projection inequality is

  (x-g) dot (z-g)<=0 for every z in D.                 (2.1)

It follows either by differentiating the squared distance along the segment
from g to z, or conversely by expanding ||x-z||^2-||x-g||^2. Thus (2.1)
is necessary and sufficient and supplies a direct check of every guard below.

For two inputs x,y and projections g,p, add (2.1) with z=p and z=g to get

  ||g-p||^2<=(g-p) dot (x-y)<=||g-p|| ||x-y||.

Hence projection is1-Lipschitz. The maximizing inequalities give, for an
increment u,

  g dot u <= F(x+u)-F(x) <= P_D(x+u) dot u.

Their difference is at most||u||^2, proving differentiability with gradient
g and smoothness1. Convexity follows from F being a maximum of affine
functions of x. The function is finite everywhere because D is compact.

Since0 belongs to D, F>=0 and F(0)=0. For x!=0 choose
0<t<min{1,1/(2||x||)}. Then tx belongs to D and
F(x)>=(t-t^2/2)||x||^2>0. Thus the complete minimum set is exactly{0}.
The true initial distance is ||x_0||; there is no unused carrier or selectable
closer minimum.

For all original samples i=0,...,n let g_i=P_D(x_i), f_i=F(x_i), and add
the optimum sample x_*=g_*=0,f_*=0. Set z_j=x_j-g_j. Since
f_i=x_i dot g_i-||g_i||^2/2, direct expansion gives, for EVERY ordered pair,

  Q_ij := f_i-f_j+g_i dot(x_j-x_i)+||g_i-g_j||^2/2
        = (g_i-g_j) dot z_j <=0.                     (2.2)

The last inequality is (2.1) for g_j and z=g_i. This includes every pair
with the terminal n and every pair involving *. No reduced row family or
terminal replacement is being used.

For any spatial scale s>0,
F_(sD)(x)=s^2 F_D(x/s). Thus the run from s x_0 is the scale-s version
of this run, and its normalized payoff is identical. Multiplication of F
by any L>0, with steps h_i/L, also preserves the points and normalized
payoff. The report uses the original W=2R normalization throughout.

## 3. Seven closed projection regions, with every guard

There are seven face labels: C for the whole triangle, E_i for an edge,
and V_i for a vertex. Associate to each a symmetric orthogonal projection
matrix P_f, vector b_f orthogonal to its range, and closed region R_f:

  C:   P_C=I, b_C=0,
       R_C={x: -v_i dot x<=1/2 for all i};

  E_i: P_E=t_i t_i^T, b_E=n_i/2,
       R_E={x: -n_i dot x<=-1/2,
                  t_i dot x<=b, -t_i dot x<=b};

  V_i: P_V=0, b_V=v_i,
       R_V={x: (v_j-v_i) dot x<=-3/2 for both j!=i}.

On R_f the actual projection is

  P_D(x)=P_f x+b_f,                                 (3.1)
  2F(x)=x^T P_f x+2b_f dot x-||b_f||^2.            (3.2)

For C this is x itself. For E_i write x=z n_i+u t_i: the guards are
z>=1/2, |u|<=b, and (3.1) is n_i/2+u t_i. Its residual is
(z-1/2)n_i and (2.1) follows from n_i dot g<=1/2 on D. For V_i,
(2.1) for the other two vertices is exactly the two displayed guards;
linearity gives it for their entire convex hull. Conversely each projection
lies in the interior of D, in an edge, or at a vertex, giving one of these
seven regions by (2.1). Shared boundaries are permitted: the formulas agree
there because the projection is unique. These facts prove both coverage
and the absence of a spurious branch.

Formula (3.2) follows by inserting (3.1) into x dot g-||g||^2/2 and using
P_f^2=P_f=P_f^T and P_f b_f=0. It remains valid at every shared boundary.

For orientation only, an alternative full two-coordinate description uses
q_i=(2/3)x dot v_i, with sum q_i=0 and
||x||^2=(3/2)sum q_i^2. If A=max q_i and B=-min q_i, then
A/2<=B<=2A and the ordered triple is(A,B-A,-B). The core guard is
B<=1/3; the vertex guard is2A-B>=1; otherwise the two upper coordinates
form the active edge. The next ordered triple must actually be sorted
again after an overrelaxed step. Nothing in this report presumes that its
old order persists or that equal coordinates can split.

## 4. Every physical prefix and the complete initial core

For a positive integer q let nu_2(q) be the largest integer r>=0 for which
2^r divides q. For an integer ell>=0 let sbit(ell) be the number of ones
in its binary expansion. The original ruler word satisfies

  h_(q-1)-1=a c^(nu_2(q))=beta c^(nu_2(q)-1),
                      1<=q<=n.                    (4.1)

Indeed the bridge of H_(j+1) is at q=2^j, and for0<r<2^j the right
child has nu_2(2^j+r)=nu_2(r). This proves (4.1) by induction on the
literal concatenation.

For every physical prefix length1<=ell<=n,

  sum_(q=1)^ell nu_2(q)=sum_(r>=1) floor(ell/2^r)
                     =ell-sbit(ell),
  p_ell:=product_(i=0)^(ell-1)(h_i-1)
         =beta^ell c^(-sbit(ell))<=beta/c=a<1/2.      (4.2)

To prove the second counting identity write ell as sum e_j2^j. Each bit
contributes sum_(r=1)^j 2^(j-r)=2^j-1 to the floor sum. All sums are finite.
The bound uses beta<1, sbit(ell)>=1, and c>1+sqrt(2)>2.

Set p_0=1 and p=p_n=beta^n c^(-m). If x_0 belongs to D, then

  x_ell=(-1)^ell p_ell x_0, 0<=ell<=n.               (4.3)

This is a genuine induction on the physical updates: for every nonempty
prefix a positive scale <=a maps D into D, while a negative scale of
magnitude <=a maps D into2aD subset D. Thus each point predicted by (4.3)
is in D, its actual projection is itself, and the next update gives (4.3)
again. This checks every intervening prefix, including those containing
large bridges. It is not an inference from the final product alone.

Consequently every nonzero x_0 in D has

  E_m(x_0)=p^2=beta^(2n)c^(-2m).                     (4.4)

For later comparisons derive the mass formula within this joint draft.
Put S_j=sum H_j, A_j=1+S_j, and v_mass=a/(c-2). The recursion gives
A_(j+1)=2A_j+a c^j and hence

  A_j=(1-v_mass)2^j+v_mass c^j.                     (4.5)

Substitution checks the initial value and every step. Since
lambda(lambda-2)=1, c>lambda and beta<1 imply0<v_mass<1. For j>=1,
A_j<c^j. Therefore D_m=2A_m-1<2c^m<c^(2m), and

  p^2<1/D_m.                                      (4.6)

The middle strict inequality uses c^m>2.

## 5. Full fixed-face classes: exact terminal scores and own radii

A fixed-face class here requires the projection to belong to the designated
closed face at every original query AND at the actual terminal. Shared
boundary labels cause no difficulty.

### 5.1 A fixed vertex

Fix a vertex v. Let its normal cone be
N_D(v)={w: w dot(g-v)<=0 for every g in D}.
The full fixed-vertex class is exactly

  x_0=(S+1)v+w, w in N_D(v).                       (5.1)

Necessity follows by summing the constant gradient v and using the terminal
vertex guard. Sufficiency holds because every prefix has
x_i=(1+S-s_i)v+w, where s_i=sum_(t<i)h_t, and v belongs to N_D(v).
Thus the residual w+(S-s_i)v stays in that cone. All the guards hold.

Write t=v dot w>=0 and w=t v+w_perp, with w_perp perpendicular to v.
The nonnegative sign follows by testing g=0 in the normal inequality.
The actual terminal is v+w and

  E_m(x_0)=(1+2t)/[(S+1+t)^2+||w_perp||^2]
          <=1/D_m.                                (5.2)

Indeed (S+1+t)^2-D_m(1+2t)=(t-S)^2. Equality is attained at
w=S v, which is legal, giving x_0=D_m v. No transverse coordinate was
dropped from the denominator in (5.2).

### 5.2 A fixed edge

Fix its orthonormal n,t as in Section1 and write x_0=z_0 n+u_0 t.
The full fixed-edge class is exactly

  z_0>=(S+1)/2, |u_0|<=b.                          (5.3)

Necessity follows from the initial and terminal edge guards and the normal
update. For sufficiency each physical prefix is

  z_i=z_0-s_i/2>=1/2,
  u_i=(-1)^i p_i u_0,

whose tangential guards follow from p_0=1 and (4.2). Thus these are the
actual updates and the terminal remains on the same edge region. By (3.2),

  E_m(x_0)=[z_0-D_m/4+p^2 u_0^2]/[z_0^2+u_0^2]
          <=1/D_m.                                (5.4)

The normal inequality is z_0^2-D_m(z_0-D_m/4)=(z_0-D_m/2)^2>=0;
the tangential inequality is (4.6). Equality holds at u_0=0,z_0=D_m/2,
which satisfies (5.3). Therefore

  V_triangle(m)>=1/D_m.                            (5.5)

These exact fixed-face optima do not bound histories that change faces.
In particular (5.5), combined with accepted931's B_n/D_m<47/50, is NOT
an upper bound on B_n V_triangle(m).

## 6. A legal-prefix obstruction to the radial envelope shortcut

A tempting one-step ingredient for propagating the inscribed-ball radius
would be

  ||x-h P_D(x)||<=max{h-1, ||x||-h/2}, h>=1.        (FALSE)

It is false for every h>2, including an actual bridge of the fixed word.
Use one edge frame n,t and choose its endpoint v=n/2+b t. Put

  x=2h n+b t, r=||x||=sqrt(4h^2+3/4).

The edge/vertex boundary guard is exact, so P_D(x)=v. Its next point is
(2h-h/2)n+(1-h)b t. Direct symbolic expansion gives

  ||x-hv||^2-(r-h/2)^2
     =h(r-2h)+(3/4)h(h-2)>0.                       (6.1)

Also r-h/2>=3h/2>h-1, so the right side of the proposed envelope is
r-h/2. This proves the failure, with an explicit transverse component.

To realize this at an actual original query, use the level2 bridge
h=1+a c^2=1+beta c. Here beta>3/4 and c>12/5, so h>2. This is physical
query3, preceded by H_2. Initialize at

  x_0=x+S_2 v.

The residual x-v=(2h-1/2)n is in N_D(v), and adding any nonnegative
multiple of v preserves that cone. Thus every preceding gradient is v,
and summing those actual steps lands at x at query3. The same static F
then defines every remaining original point and row by Section2; no
claim about its later payoff is made in this counterexample.

This refutes the radial-envelope proof ingredient, not V_triangle=1/D_m
and not a full-function upper bound. The second method below retains the
actual coordinates and does not use this failed envelope.

## 7. Compactness and an explicit finite guard list for every history

First reduce the unrestricted initial radius without losing an optimizer.
Since ||P_D(x)||<=1, every actual run obeys

  ||x_n||<=||x_0||+S, F(x_n)<=||x_n||,
  E_m(x_0)<=2(r+S)/r^2, r=||x_0||.                 (7.1)

For r>=R:=4D_m, the last quantity is strictly less than1/D_m. One way
to check this is that r^2-2D_m r-2D_m S is increasing for r>=4D_m,
and at4D_m it equals7D_m^2+D_m>0. Meanwhile the punctured ball of
radius1/2 is covered by (4.4) and has the strictly smaller value (4.6).
A point attaining1/D_m exists by (5.2). The unrestricted maximum is
therefore attained in the compact annulus1/2<=r<=R.

It is harmless to use the containing square

  K_R={x: -R<=x_1<=R, -R<=x_2<=R}

for the finite formula: it contains a global optimizer and every extra
point is still a legal original initial point.

Let alpha=(sigma_0,...,sigma_n) range over all7^(n+1) strings of the seven face
labels. There is a label at the terminal n. Define literal affine products
from the original h, with empty products equal to I:

  U_i=I-h_i P_(sigma_i),
  M_0=I, e_0=0,
  M_i=U_(i-1) ... U_0,
  e_i=-sum_(s=0)^(i-1) h_s [U_(i-1) ... U_(s+1)] b_(sigma_s).
                                                        (7.2)

These are finite written products and sums, not executed recurrences.
Every U_i is invertible: its eigenvalues are1 and/or1-h_i, with h_i>1.
In particular each M_i is invertible.

Write the individual guards of Section3 as r_guard dot y<=t_guard. Pull every such
guard at time i back to the same original input x:

  (M_i^T r_guard) dot x <= t_guard-r_guard dot e_i. (7.3)

Adjoin the four square guards. This gives a fully specified finite list
(c_l,d_l), l=1,...,L_alpha, with c_l in R^2, d_l real. Each c_l is
nonzero, since the original normals are nonzero and M_i is invertible.
Let

  C_alpha={x: c_l dot x<=d_l for every l}.          (7.4)

This notation describes the proof, not an unevaluated feasibility oracle:
Sections8--9 give explicit points and literal sign tests, so no search for
an x satisfying (7.4) is left in the final expression.

If x satisfies (7.3), the actual history equals M_i x+e_i by induction:
the selected projection is the actual one, and its update is
U_i y-h_i b_(sigma_i).
Conversely every actual history has such a label at every time and hence
belongs to some C_alpha. Shared boundary histories may have several
labels, but the actual points and objective agree.

If sigma_0=C, then x belongs to D, all actual points are in D by Section4,
and the payoff is p^2. All these strings may be skipped. If sigma_0!=C,
the initial edge or vertex guard gives ||x||>=1/2; thus C_alpha stays
away from0, even when it is lower dimensional. Every C_alpha is compact
because the square guards are included.

## 8. Explicit vertex and edge candidates; no continuous maximization

For one string with sigma_0!=C abbreviate
M=M_n,d=e_n,P=P_(sigma_n),b_0=b_(sigma_n).
By (3.2) the actual numerator on C_alpha is the quadratic

  q_alpha(x)=x^T A x+2ell dot x+k,
  A=M^T P M,
  ell=M^T(Pd+b_0),
  k=d^T P d+2b_0 dot d-||b_0||^2.                 (8.1)

The exact payoff is q_alpha(x)/||x||^2. Define a sign filter on any
explicit point z: retain it precisely when c_l dot z<=d_l for every
l and ||z||^2>0. These are finitely many specified real-number comparisons.

Define Root2(A_0,B_0,C_0) as follows. If A_0!=0 and
Delta=B_0^2-4A_0C_0>=0, list(-B_0+sqrt(Delta))/(2A_0) and
(-B_0-sqrt(Delta))/(2A_0). If A_0=0,B_0!=0, list -C_0/B_0.
Otherwise list nothing. Repeated roots may be kept once. The identically
zero polynomial is handled in the proofs below and contributes no roots.

### 8.1 Vertices

For every pair l<r whose row normals are linearly independent, solve the
two linear equations by the displayed inverse

  z= [c_l^T; c_r^T]^(-1) [d_l; d_r].               (8.2)

Retain it if it passes the sign filter. These candidates include every
vertex of a nonempty compact polygon C_alpha, including a singleton.
Matrix inversion in (8.2) means the explicit two-by-two adjugate divided
by its nonzero determinant; it is not a solver invocation.

### 8.2 Stationary points on each guard line

For each guard c dot x=d_0 put

  C_0=||c||^2>0, u=d_0^2/C_0,
  z_0=(d_0/C_0)c, v=Jc.

The line is x=z_0+t v, z_0 dot v=0, ||v||^2=C_0. Put

  a_e=v^T A v,
  b_e=v dot(Az_0+ell),
  c_e=z_0^T A z_0+2ell dot z_0+k.

Its ratio is

  (a_e t^2+2b_e t+c_e)/(u+C_0 t^2).

For every root returned by

  Root2(-b_e C_0, a_e u-c_e C_0, b_e u),            (8.3)

form z=z_0+t v and apply the sign filter. This list includes every
nonconstant stationary point in the relative interior of a legal edge.
Indeed differentiating the ratio gives twice the polynomial

  -b_e C_0 t^2+(a_e u-c_e C_0)t+b_e u

divided by the positive squared denominator. If the guard line passes
through0, a generated point at0 is discarded; C_alpha itself cannot
contain0. If this polynomial vanishes identically, the ratio is constant
on the connected feasible segment, and its endpoints have the same value
and are already covered by (8.2). Compactness supplies those endpoints.
This also handles a one-dimensional C_alpha.

## 9. Interior candidates and the singular case

At an interior stationary point x!=0 let z=q_alpha(x)/||x||^2 be its
value. Differentiating in both coordinates gives

  (A-zI)x=-ell,
  ell dot x+k=0.                                  (9.1)

If det(A-zI)!=0, these equations give the explicit candidate

  x=-(A-zI)^(-1)ell                               (9.2)

and the polynomial equation

  Pi(z):=k det(A-zI)-ell^T adj(A-zI)ell=0.         (9.3)

This has degree at most two. Its coefficients can be written without a
formal determinant symbol. If
A=[A_11 A_12; A_12 A_22] and ell=(ell_1,ell_2), then

  Pi(z)= k z^2
       +[-k(A_11+A_22)+ell_1^2+ell_2^2] z
       +k(A_11 A_22-A_12^2)
        -A_22 ell_1^2+2A_12 ell_1ell_2-A_11 ell_2^2.  (9.4)

Use Root2 on these three coefficients. For each listed real z with
nonzero det(A-zI), form (9.2) and retain it under the sign filter. Equations
(9.1) then hold, and the ratio at this point is exactly z.

If Pi is identically zero, its quadratic coefficient gives k=0 and its
linear coefficient then gives ||ell||^2=0. Thus (9.2) would only give0,
which is excluded. No nonsingular interior stationary candidate is missed
by letting Root2 return no roots in this case.

It remains to justify discarding singular interior stationary values.
Suppose x is interior, (9.1) holds, and A-zI is singular. Pick a nonzero
w in its kernel. Symmetry and (A-zI)x=-ell imply ell dot w=0. For every
real t, a direct expansion gives

  q_alpha(x+t w)-z||x+t w||^2=0.                  (9.5)

For example the coefficient of t^2 vanishes by the kernel condition,
the linear coefficient vanishes by (9.1), and the constant term is zero
by the definition of z. Intersect the line x+R w with the compact polygon.
It contains a nontrivial segment about x and has boundary endpoints.
The polygon is separated from0, so the ratios there are defined and are
also z by (9.5). Those endpoints are covered by the boundary reasoning
in Section8. If A=zI and ell=k=0, the ratio is constant everywhere,
and any polygon vertex suffices. This proves that no singular stationary
family requires an additional feasibility problem or free parameter.

## 10. The exact finite full-profile expression

Let Z_alpha be the finite list of all points retained from (8.2), (8.3),
and (9.2). It is generated solely by the literal products (7.2),
nonzero determinant divisions, Root2, and the explicit sign filter.
Empty lists contribute no value. Define the finite set of real numbers

  L_m={p^2,1/D_m}
      union over all alpha with sigma_0!=C
             {q_alpha(z)/||z||^2: z in Z_alpha}.     (10.1)

Then the exact whole-initial-state identity is

  V_triangle(m)=max L_m.                            (10.2)

Proof of the upper direction: a global maximum exists in the square by
Section7. If its initial label is C, its value is p^2. Otherwise it is a
maximum of the continuous ratio over some C_alpha. If that polygon is a
point or a line, Section8 supplies a candidate of the same value. In two

## 6. Mechanism2: exact monotone ray segments and a single crossing

The estimates in this section are proved jointly and used below; they
are not imported from the earlier unverified common-curvature report.

Consider any segment staying on one ray of positive curvature p and
threshold u, with physical mass T. Let its initial and terminal radii
be r and z. Radii are nonincreasing along such a segment because every
update is inward and, by assumption, does not cross. Every queried
gradient magnitude is at least p*min(z,u). Thus

    r>=z+p*T*min(z,u).                              (6.1)

If z<=u, twice the terminal objective is p*z^2, and (6.1) gives
the bound p*r^2/(1+p*T)^2<=p*r^2/(1+2*p*T).
If z>=u, twice the objective is p*(2*u*z-u^2); the identity

    (z+p*T*u)^2-(1+2*p*T)*(2*u*z-u^2)
       =(z-(1+p*T)*u)^2>=0                         (6.2)

gives the same upper bound. The tie z=u is included in both formulas.
Hence every such segment satisfies

    2*f(terminal)<=p*r^2/(1+2*p*T).                 (6.3)

When all steps in a block satisfy h*p<=1, its ray radius map is exactly
the chronological composition of

    r -> r-h*p*min(r,u), r>=0.                     (6.4)

Each map is nonnegative, nondecreasing, piecewise affine with slopes
1-h*p and1, and at most its input. Thus this is a genuinely monotone
one-side block, including h*p=1. Inequality (6.3) controls its true
terminal energy whether the terminal is quadratic or clipped.

Now consider a history with exactly one strict sign crossing. Let
its source and destination curvatures be p and v, its crossing step
be h, and its physical prefix and suffix masses be P,T. The entire
prefix is on the source ray. For pre-crossing radius y, write
w=min(y,u_source), so the query gradient magnitude is p*w.
If the initial radius is R, monotonicity of the prefix gives

    R>=y+p*P*w>=(1+p*P)*w.

The crossing requires h*p>1 and has landing radius

    z=h*p*w-y<=(h*p-1)*w
                    <=[(h*p-1)/(1+p*P)]*R.        (6.5)

Its suffix stays on the destination ray. Combining (6.3) and (6.5),

    2*f(terminal)/R^2
       <=[v/(1+2*v*T)]*[(h*p-1)/(1+p*P)]^2.        (6.6)

These source-to-destination factors use the true two curvatures.
The derivatives of the positive factors with respect to their own
curvatures are

    d/dv [v/(1+2*v*T)]=1/(1+2*v*T)^2,
    d/dp [(h*p-1)/(1+p*P)]=(h+P)/(1+p*P)^2.

They are positive. Thus if both curvatures are at most K, (6.6) is
at most its expression with both parameters replaced by K. This is
monotonicity of a proved scalar upper expression; it asserts no
curvature monotonicity of actual GD trajectories.

## 7. Every single crossing at every physical position of H_j

For any0<K<=1 and any level-k occurrence in H_j, a crossing with
source curvature at most K is bounded using the preceding section.
Let

    C=1+K*S_k, e=K*h_k^lev-1.

If e<=0 no curvature at most K crosses there. Otherwise e>0 and

    e/C<=d_k/A_k<c-2<1/2.                          (7.1)

For the first inequality, the ratio
(K*h_k^lev-1)/(1+K*S_k) increases in K and is d_k/A_k at K=1.

Set N=K*(S_j-S_(k+1))>=0 and x=K*(P-S_k). By (3.4),0<=x<=N and

    (1+K*P)^2*(1+2*K*T)
       =(C+x)^2*(2*C-1+2*N-2*x).                  (7.2)

The derivative of the right side with respect to x is
2*(C+x)*(C-1+2*N-3*x). Its sign can change only from positive to
negative. Therefore its minimum on[0,N] is at an endpoint. The
value at N minus the value at0 is

    N*(2*C*(C-1)+N*(2*C-1))>=0.

Consequently (7.2) is at least C^2*(2*C-1+2*N). On the other hand,

    1+2*K*S_j=4*C+2*e-1+2*N.

Using e/C<1/2 and C>=1,

    e^2*(4*C+2*e-1)/(C^2*(2*C-1))
       <(5*C-1)/(4*(2*C-1))<=1.                   (7.3)

The last inequality is equivalent to3*(C-1)>=0. Adding the2*N
terms preserves the required inequality because e^2<C^2. It follows

    e^2/[(1+K*P)^2*(1+2*K*T)]
          <=1/(1+2*K*S_j).                         (7.4)

Together with (6.6), this proves the following complete conditional
history bound: on ANY H_j with the fixed enclosing-m parameters, a
history having at most one strict sign crossing satisfies

    2*f(Psi_j(s))/s^2<=K/(1+2*K*S_j).               (7.5)

A no-crossing history follows from (6.3) and monotonicity of

zero terminal gap, so it does not create a missing crossing case.
For j=0, (7.5) is the immediate 2*f(s)<=K*s^2. This includes both
leaves at the ends of every nonempty word and every possible cut.

One further radius estimate will pay for the root return. A FIRST

       <=d_k/(1+P)<=d_k/A_k<c-2.                  (7.6)

The middle comparison again follows by increasing p to1 in this
positive upper expression. This is a first-crossing bound, not a
claim of radial contraction under an arbitrary returning suffix.

## 8. Split at the first level where both signs can reverse

Reflect the fixed function if necessary so that the ray of curvature
q is negative and the ray of curvature K is positive. Reflection also
exchanges the two fixed clipping levels and all starts, and leaves the
profile unchanged. If the curvatures tie, either labeling is allowed.

Define the first common reversing level

    J_q=min{j in{0,...,m-1}: q*h_j^lev>1},

also permits a core reversal on the K-ray. The strict inequality is

The first common reversing level is either J_q=m-1 or infinity.

In the root case the complete physical word is exactly

    H_j, h_j^lev, H_j.

## 9. The root return, including a preceding and a following crossing

If no negative-to-positive crossing occurs, a nonzero full history

then gives the sharp upper bound. Zero hits have zero gap as before.

Otherwise the sole negative-to-positive crossing is the root. Let

    e_q=q*h_j^lev-1>0, j=m-1.

The strict step-ratio comparison follows from

attainment let the K-ray threshold be u_high=b_high/K, and set

    D_K=1+2*K*S_m, s=D_K*u_high

on that ray. For every physical prefix mass P_i=sum_(t<i)h_t, the

    x_i=u_high*(D_K-K*P_i), 0<=i<=n_m.

    x_(n_m)=u_high*(1+K*S_m),

and x_0!=x_star, under x_(i+1)=x_i-(h_i/L)grad f(x_i). Thus W=2R.

    C_0=B_0=1,
